courseMetadata.title: Back End Architecture Design for Front End Engineers
courseMetadata.description: An intermediate, project-driven course that converts working front end engineers into engineers who can design, build, defend, and operate server-side systems. Across eight sections you build and repeatedly refactor one real system — Meridian, a venue booking platform — under increasing constraints: concurrency, contracts, persistence, database internals, caching and identity, service decomposition, distributed correctness, and production readiness. Every section pairs an architectural decision space with a hands-on build, so you finish with a running multi-service system and the vocabulary to defend its design in a code review, a design review, or a system design interview.

prerequisites.description: Comfortable writing JavaScript or TypeScript, including async/await and promises. You should be able to explain what happens when you await a promise.
Working familiarity with HTTP: methods, status codes, headers, and request/response bodies. You have consumed REST APIs from a client.
Basic SQL: you can write a SELECT with a JOIN and a WHERE clause, even if you have never designed a schema.
Command-line comfort: running a local server, installing packages, and using curl or an equivalent HTTP client.
No prior server-side architecture experience is assumed. The course explicitly builds on front end intuitions and corrects the places where they do not transfer.

interleavingGroups.rationaleNote: The single strongest thread in the course: a module-level variable (s1), a contended database row (s3), a cache key missing an input (s4), and a cross-machine race (s8) are the same failure at four scopes. Interleaving these forces learners to recognise the pattern rather than the setting, which is exactly what the transfer requirement tests.

Expand/contract is one shape applied at three layers: API fields, schema columns, and message schemas. Learners who meet it only once treat it as a database technique; interleaving reveals it as the general answer to 'change a thing while people depend on it'.

Idempotency is introduced as a contract obligation (s2), becomes the precondition for safe retries (s5), is forced by at-least-once outbox delivery (s7), and finally makes replay a routine tool (s8). This is the most reinforced idea in the course and the one most often half-learned.

Isolation levels (s3), staleness windows (s4), replication lag (s7), and formal consistency models (s8) are one ladder. Interleaving them prevents the common terminal error of treating 'strong consistency' as a global setting rather than a per-operation choice.

CPU-vs-I/O (s1), Little's Law pool sizing (s7), capacity estimation (s5), and SLO error budgets (s6) all train the same reflex: find the binding constraint with a number before proposing a change. Interleaved retrieval here directly attacks the 'just add servers' misconception.

A contract boundary, a trust boundary, and a service boundary are three views of the same line. Learners who separate them enforce authorization at the gateway and leak storage into the API; interleaving keeps the three questions attached to each other.

Designing for failure and being able to see failure are the same competency split across design time and run time. Retrieval items about timeouts and circuit breakers injected into the observability experience force learners to connect the design to the metric that would reveal it.

Every irreversible decision in the course — storage engine, topology, partition key, consistency model, analytical separation — is also a communication task. This group is deliberately the widest: the capstone defense in s6 must feel like the eighth repetition of an argument the learner has already made seven times, not a new genre.

probeQuestions.prompt: A server handler assigns a value to a variable declared at the **top of the module** (outside any function), then reads it back after an `await`. Two users hit this endpoint at the same time. What happens?
options: Each request gets its own copy of the variable, so both are correct.
The second request waits until the first finishes, so both are correct.
The second request can overwrite the value between the first request's assignment and its read, so one user can receive the other's data.
The runtime raises a concurrent-modification error.

optionFeedback.feedback: Only variables declared *inside* the function are per-invocation. A module-level variable is shared by every request that instance serves.
Requests are not serialised. An await hands control to other pending work, which is exactly when the shared value changes.
Correct. This is the defining difference between browser code and server code: one process, many concurrent users, so module-level mutable state is shared state.
No such error exists. The failure is silent, which is what makes it dangerous — it produces wrong data rather than a crash.

routingRules.action: Mark `server-runtime-model` as provisionally strong. Section 1's shared-state experience may be skimmed, but the learner should still complete the loop-blocking activity, which tests a different objective.
Route to Section 1 in full and flag `server-runtime-model.m1` for early remediation. Do not allow skipping Section 1 experiences.

probeQuestions.prompt: An endpoint takes 3 seconds. Instrumentation shows the single database query it runs completes in 11ms. What is the most likely cause?
options: A missing index on the queried table.
Time spent queuing — for the event loop, or for a free database connection — rather than in the query itself.
Slow client network connections.
The database server needs more memory.

optionFeedback.feedback: The query already completes in 11ms, so there is no index problem to solve. This is the most common misdiagnosis in backend work.
Correct. Latency is queuing delay plus service time across several hops. The query is only one of them, and often not the guilty one.
Server-side timing largely excludes client network time, and a consistent 3 seconds across many clients points inside your system.
Nothing in the symptoms suggests memory pressure, and the query itself is already fast.

routingRules.action: Learner already reasons about queuing. Section 1 lecture content may be read at speed; still require the fault-localization activity in Section 8.
Emphasise the six-hop lifecycle diagram in Section 1 and require the injected-fault exercise before Section 4 (`s7-database-systems`).

probeQuestions.prompt: Your API returns `"weight": 2.4` in kilograms and you must now support pounds, changing the field to an object with a value and a unit. What is the right first move?
options: Ship `/v2/shipments` with the new shape.
Change the field in place and notify clients in the release notes.
Add the new field alongside the existing one, deprecate the old one with a date, and measure who still reads it before removing it.
Add a query parameter so clients can request the new shape.

optionFeedback.feedback: A version bump duplicates your entire surface indefinitely, including the endpoints that did not change. It is the last resort, not the first move.
This is a breaking change to a field's type. Existing clients will fail regardless of what the release notes say.
Correct. Expand, announce and instrument, migrate, then contract — and the measurement step is what makes removal possible at all.
Workable as a transition mechanism, but it does not address the deprecation and removal path, and it makes the parameter itself permanent contract.

routingRules.action: Unlock the advanced contract-evolution transfer exercise in Section 2 and reduce the guided worked example to a summary.
Require the full expand/contract worked example and the four-phase planning activity in Section 2.

probeQuestions.prompt: You add an index to speed up a slow query on a table receiving 20,000 writes per second. What is the honest tradeoff?
options: There is no tradeoff; indexes only affect reads.
Every insert and update must also maintain the index, so at this write volume the cost may exceed the read benefit.
The index will consume memory but will not affect write throughput.
The tradeoff is only storage space.

optionFeedback.feedback: Indexes are additional structures the database must keep current on every write to the table.
Correct. An index trades write throughput and storage for read selectivity on specific queries, and at high write volume that trade can be a net loss.
Memory is one cost, but write throughput is the one that matters at 20,000 writes per second.
Storage is the least significant of the three costs here.

routingRules.action: Section 3's indexing worked example may be compressed; still require the measured write-cost activity, which produces the numbers used later.
Require the zero/one/four-index write-throughput measurement in Section 3 before proceeding to `s7-database-systems`.

probeQuestions.prompt: Your application writes to its database and then writes the same change to a search index. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing, as long as both writes are awaited and errors are logged.
The search index may briefly lag, but the two will converge on their own.
If the second write fails there is nothing to roll back, so the two disagree permanently, silently, with no detection.
The database write may fail after the index write, leaving an orphaned index entry.

optionFeedback.feedback: Logging the error records that something went wrong; it does not fix the divergence, and nobody reads that log line.
There is no convergence mechanism. Nothing re-attempts the failed write or reconciles the two systems.
Correct. This is the dual-write problem, and its defining property is silent, permanent divergence discovered weeks later by a customer.
This is a real ordering concern, but it is the smaller case; the dangerous one is the first write succeeding and the second failing.

routingRules.action: Unlock the CDC-versus-outbox comparison as an extension activity in `s7-database-systems`.
Require the dual-write failure demonstration in `s7-database-systems` before the outbox build.

probeQuestions.prompt: A handler runs `if (user.role === 'manager') { return bookingsForVenue(venueId); }`. What is the problem?
options: It should check authentication before authorization.
It authorizes the role but not the resource, so any manager can read any venue's bookings.
It should return 403 rather than silently returning data.
Nothing is wrong, provided the gateway has already authenticated the caller.

optionFeedback.feedback: Authentication is presumably already established, since `user` exists. The gap is elsewhere.
Correct. This is an insecure direct object reference. The check must compare the resource's owner to the caller, which means it can only happen after fetching the resource.
Status codes matter, but the vulnerability is that unauthorised data is returned at all.
The gateway cannot know who owns a particular venue. Resource-level authorization must live with the resource.

routingRules.action: Learner has the resource-authorization instinct. Section 5's authorization lecture may be skimmed, but the self-attack activity remains mandatory.
Flag `security-authn-authz.m2` as high priority. Require the curl self-attack exercise and a full authorization sweep in `s6-production-readiness-review`.

probeQuestions.prompt: A payment call times out after 2 seconds. What do you know?
options: The request did not reach the payment service.
The request failed, so it is safe to retry.
You do not know whether the charge happened — the request may have succeeded with the response lost.
The payment service is down.

optionFeedback.feedback: A timeout tells you nothing about arrival. The request may have arrived and been fully processed.
It is not safe to retry without an idempotency key, precisely because the original may have succeeded.
Correct. The ambiguous timeout is the defining problem of distributed systems, and an idempotency key is what resolves it.
It may be down, or merely slow, or perfectly healthy behind a slow network. The timeout does not distinguish these.

routingRules.action: Mark `reliability-failure-design` as provisionally strong and unlock the circuit-breaker and bulkhead extension in Section 6.
Require the double-charge demonstration in Section 6 before the saga work in `s8-distributed-programming`.

probeQuestions.prompt: Your team of seven is starting a new product. Someone proposes microservices from day one. What is the strongest consideration?
options: Microservices scale better, so starting with them avoids a painful migration.
Microservices primarily solve team-autonomy problems, which a seven-person team does not have.
It depends on expected request volume; above a certain threshold microservices are required.
It is fine as long as each service has its own database.

optionFeedback.feedback: The benefits are organisational rather than performance-related, and early boundaries are usually wrong — far cheaper to fix inside one deployable.
Correct. A modular monolith gives the boundary discipline that makes later extraction mechanical, at a fraction of the distributed cost.
The trigger is organisational, not volumetric. A high-traffic system run by one team is often best as a monolith.
Separate databases are a necessary condition for a good split, not a reason to split.

routingRules.action: Unlock the extended topology-decision transfer exercise in Section 6 and compress the comparison-table walkthrough.
Require the three-staffing-scenario decision activity in Section 6 and introduce the modular monolith explicitly.

probeQuestions.prompt: Which statement about the CAP theorem is accurate?
options: You choose two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.
Partitions are unavoidable, so the real choice is between availability and consistency during a partition.
Modern databases have solved CAP and provide all three.
CAP applies only to NoSQL databases.

optionFeedback.feedback: Partition tolerance is not something you can decline. Networks partition whether or not you chose it.
Correct. PACELC extends this with the choice that applies the rest of the time: latency versus consistency when there is no partition, which is where you actually live.
No system evades the theorem. What modern systems offer is finer-grained, per-operation control over the trade.
It applies to any replicated data store, relational or otherwise.

routingRules.action: Unlock the quorum-analysis extension in `s8-distributed-programming` and reduce the CAP explanation to a recap.
Require the full CAP/PACELC treatment and the six-operation consistency-assignment activity in `s8-distributed-programming`.

probeQuestions.prompt: In two or three sentences: describe a time you were **blocked, surprised, or burned** by a backend system you did not control — a slow API, a confusing error, a change that broke your client, data that was out of date. What did you need to know that you could not find out?
scoringCriteria: Describes a specific incident rather than a general frustration.
Identifies what information was missing, not only what went wrong.
Not scored for correctness — this is an anchoring exercise whose answer is returned to the learner in the final section.

routingRules.action: Store verbatim and surface it in `s6-production-readiness-review` alongside the ADR activity, so the learner writes the document that would have answered their own past question.

routingRules.condition: Response mentions stale or out-of-date data
routingRules.action: Prioritise the staleness-window material in `s4-state-caching-identity` and tag `state-caching-consistency.m3` for early attention.

routingRules.condition: Response mentions a breaking API change
routingRules.action: Prioritise the expand/contract material in `s2-api-contracts` and use the learner's own example in the section's motivation hook.

competencies.title: Server runtime and request lifecycle reasoning
competencies.description: Reason about how a server process accepts, schedules, and completes concurrent requests: event loops versus thread pools, process and instance topology, statelessness, and where request-scoped work actually lives. Includes locating where latency accumulates across the six hops from browser to database and back.

desiredOutcomes.description: Trace an HTTP request end to end and name the hop responsible for an observed latency, distinguishing queuing delay from service time.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner names at least four of the six hops in order and, given a latency profile, selects the correct hop with a reason that references queuing rather than guessing at the query.

desiredOutcomes.description: Predict and repair concurrency bugs caused by shared module-level state in a multi-tenant process.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner produces an interleaving timeline showing how two requests corrupt each other across an await boundary, then refactors to request-scoped or externalized state.

desiredOutcomes.description: Classify handler work as CPU-bound or I/O-bound and select the matching concurrency remedy.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Given a workload, learner computes per-instance CPU demand against 1000ms/sec of capacity and proposes offloading or replication rather than an I/O-oriented fix.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The backend is just my frontend code without a DOM.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The runtime looks familiar, but the tenancy is completely different. One server process serves many users concurrently and stays up for weeks, so module-level mutable state is shared state, not per-user state, and every piece of mutable data needs an explicit owner.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner run twenty concurrent requests against a handler that stores per-request data in a module variable, count the mismatched responses, then run the same twenty sequentially and observe zero failures. The contrast between the two runs is what makes the tenancy difference stick; follow with the rule that any module-level mutable value read across an await boundary is a bug.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Node is single-threaded, so it fundamentally can't scale.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Concurrency comes from non-blocking I/O plus horizontal process replication, not from threads. A single event loop can hold tens of thousands of concurrent I/O-bound requests because waiting releases the loop. The real ceiling is CPU-bound work inside a handler, which is exclusive and unshareable.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Show a healthy single process holding 8,000 concurrent long-poll connections, then inject 60ms of synchronous CPU work per request and watch latency diverge. Make the learner compute demand (requests/sec x CPU-ms) against 1000ms of capacity per second so the constraint becomes arithmetic rather than folklore.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If an endpoint is slow, the database query must be slow.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Latency is queuing delay plus service time across at least six hops. The query is one of them and frequently not the guilty one; time is just as often lost to event-loop queuing, connection pool waits, serialization, or a blocked loop. Guessing wrong costs a week of work on the wrong layer.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Give the learner a fault-injection exercise where the query is instrumented at 11ms while the endpoint takes 3.2 seconds, and require them to name the hop before proposing a fix. Reinforce in the observability section by having them localize an injected fault using saturation metrics and traces rather than intuition.

competencies.title: API contract and boundary design
competencies.description: Design versioned, evolvable interfaces (REST, RPC, GraphQL) including resource modelling, error taxonomies, pagination, idempotency semantics, and backward-compatible change. Treats the contract as the one artefact that cannot be refactored unilaterally.

desiredOutcomes.description: Model product requirements into a complete contract: resources, verbs, success shapes, actionable error taxonomy, pagination strategy, and retry semantics.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner specifies all six elements for at least four endpoints, with machine-readable error types and a justified cursor-versus-offset choice.

desiredOutcomes.description: Classify a proposed change as breaking or additive and ship a breaking change without a version bump.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner applies the correctly-written-existing-client test, then produces a four-phase expand/contract plan that names what phase two measures and why phase four is impossible without it.

desiredOutcomes.description: Detect and remove storage leakage from a public contract.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner identifies at least three leaks (table-derived paths, sequential IDs, ORM-shaped filters, decodable cursors) and supplies a decoupled alternative for each.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A good API just mirrors the database tables.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The contract must serve client use cases and stay stable while storage evolves. Binding the two means every schema change — a rename, a split, a normalization — becomes a client-breaking change, and internal tables you never intended to support become supported forever.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner map their own API resources against their own schema and circle every difference; if nothing differs, they have leaked. Then force one schema change (splitting a column) and count how many client-visible changes result under each design.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If we use GraphQL, we don't really need to design the API.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: GraphQL relocates the design work rather than removing it. The hard problems move into schema design, resolver N+1 behaviour, and per-field authorization — and the last is harder than in REST precisely because clients compose queries you never anticipated.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner write a naive resolver for a list of items with a nested relation, run it against 50 rows, and count the queries issued. Then ask them to state, per field, who is allowed to read it — the exercise makes the relocated work concrete.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Versioning means shipping /v2 whenever we break something.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Most evolution should be additive and non-breaking. A version bump duplicates the entire surface indefinitely, including the endpoints that did not change, and it is paid for years. It is the expensive last resort, not the default tool.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Walk the learner through expand/contract on a single field: add alongside, announce and instrument, migrate consumers, then remove. Emphasise that teams skip the instrumentation phase because it has no visible output, and that skipping it makes removal unfalsifiable so the old field lives forever.

competencies.title: Data modelling and persistence design
competencies.description: Choose storage engines, model schemas and relationships, reason about indexes, execution plans, transactions and isolation, and design migrations that run safely against live traffic.

desiredOutcomes.description: Design a normalized schema and justify every denormalization with a named query, its current cost, its required cost, and its synchronization mechanism.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner produces a schema with correct cardinalities and, for each denormalization, supplies the three-part receipt plus the permanent sync obligation it creates.

desiredOutcomes.description: Diagnose a slow query from an execution plan and change indexes with the write cost stated as a number.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner reads rows-read versus rows-returned from EXPLAIN ANALYZE, proposes a composite or partial index with correct column order, and quantifies the insert-throughput cost.

desiredOutcomes.description: Sequence an expand/contract migration in which old and new code are simultaneously correct at every instant.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner produces an ordered step table distinguishing schema migrations from code deploys, uses nullable-then-backfill-then-constrain, batches the backfill, and identifies the last reversible step.

desiredOutcomes.description: Choose a transaction boundary and isolation level for a stated race condition.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner distinguishes lost update from write skew, selects locking or isolation appropriately, and excludes external network calls from the transaction boundary.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: NoSQL is faster and scales better than SQL.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The trade is access-pattern rigidity and consistency guarantees, not raw speed. A document store is fast for the access pattern its key was designed for and bad at everything else; a well-indexed relational database outperforms a badly modelled document store and can still answer questions you did not anticipate.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner list the four questions their system must answer, then attempt each against a document model keyed for only one of them. The scatter or full-scan they hit for the other three is the lesson. Reinforce that on a new product the access patterns are not yet known, which is precisely when relational optionality is worth the most.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Indexes make the database fast, so add them wherever queries are slow.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: An index trades write throughput and storage for read selectivity on specific queries. Every insert must update every index on the table, and an index no query uses is pure cost. Low-cardinality and unused indexes actively harm the system.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Make the learner measure insert throughput at zero, one, and four indexes on the same table, then report the read gain and the write cost as two numbers with a verdict. Pair with an audit of index usage counts to find indexes nothing uses.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A migration is a script you run at deploy time.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Rolling deploys mean old and new code run simultaneously for minutes, so the schema must be valid for both at every instant. An atomic cutover does not exist, and a migration that assumes one produces an outage plus an unrollbackable state.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner attempt a rename-and-split in one migration against a running load generator, observe the failures from old instances, then re-do it as the six-step expand/contract sequence and confirm every step is independently reversible.

competencies.title: Database engine internals
competencies.description: Reason about how a database executes work — page and buffer management, B-tree versus LSM storage, write-ahead logging, MVCC, vacuum and compaction, connection and pool behaviour — well enough to predict performance and diagnose incidents that are invisible at the query layer.

desiredOutcomes.description: Trace a committed write through WAL, buffer pool, and checkpoint, and predict which workloads stress which stage.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner identifies the fsync on the WAL as the durability point and explains why the data page write is deferred and amortised.

desiredOutcomes.description: Diagnose a concurrency incident from engine-level symptoms rather than query text.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Given growing disk, unchanged plans, and normal CPU, learner checks oldest-transaction age and explains the four-step chain from open transaction to degraded point lookups.

desiredOutcomes.description: Size a connection pool from throughput and in-database latency, and explain why more connections can reduce throughput.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner applies Little's Law correctly and argues that the queue must form somewhere, preferring the application over the database.

desiredOutcomes.description: Select a storage engine from the write-to-read ratio and data mutability.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner contrasts B-tree and LSM on write, read, and space amplification and names the leading operational metric to monitor for the chosen engine.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The database is a black box; I just write queries against it.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Nearly every production database incident — lock waits, version bloat, write stalls, pool exhaustion — is only diagnosable one layer below the query. Query text and execution plans are unchanged in most of these incidents, so a query-level view produces no hypothesis at all.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Give the learner an incident with growing disk usage, unchanged plans, and 25% CPU, and require a diagnosis. The query layer offers nothing, which forces them down a level. Then have them build the standing metric set: replication lag, oldest transaction age, buffer hit ratio, lock wait time, compaction backlog.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Writes are slow because disks are slow.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: In modern engines the durable write is a sequential append to a log, which is fast. The cost surfaces later and elsewhere: fsync latency, checkpoint storms, index maintenance across every index on the table, and LSM compaction. Blaming the disk sends you to the wrong four remedies.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner measure WAL bytes generated per row with zero and four indexes present, computing the write amplification ratio. Seeing the extra bytes come from index maintenance rather than the data page relocates the cost correctly.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: MVCC means readers never block writers, so concurrency is basically free.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: MVCC removes lock waits but relocates the cost into version accumulation. A single long-running transaction prevents vacuum from reclaiming any version live at its start, so dead versions pile up, reads traverse them, the buffer pool hit rate collapses, and unrelated point lookups degrade — silently and severely.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner open an idle transaction, run 200,000 updates in another session, and record table size, dead tuple count, and point-lookup latency every 30 seconds. Then have them write the causal chain in four steps with their own numbers, and add a statement timeout so the system defends itself.

competencies.title: Replication, partitioning, and data topology
competencies.description: Design multi-node data topologies: leader/follower replication, read-replica routing, replication lag, partition key selection, rebalancing, hot keys, and cross-partition queries.

desiredOutcomes.description: Design a read-replica routing policy that preserves read-your-own-writes.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner routes by required guarantee per operation rather than by read-versus-write, and names a technique that also protects the system during a bulk backfill.

desiredOutcomes.description: Choose a partition key and enumerate the queries it makes expensive plus its hot-key risk.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner tests a candidate key against both the dominant query's filter and traffic evenness, and identifies at least one query that becomes scatter-gather.

desiredOutcomes.description: Distinguish replication from backup and specify a defensible recovery position.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner explains that replication reproduces deletions and corruption at wire speed and requires point-in-time backups stored separately with tested restores.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Read replicas scale reads for free.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A replica is behind the primary — usually milliseconds, but minutes during a backfill, a large delete, or an index build. Any read whose content the user just caused breaks, so routing becomes a correctness decision rather than a load-balancing one.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner reproduce the stale-profile bug: write to the primary, redirect, read from a lagging replica, and observe the old value. Then implement all three fixes — sticky-to-primary window, log-position tokens, and lag-aware exclusion — and identify which one also saves them during a bulk backfill.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Pick a partition key with high cardinality and you're done.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The key must also match the dominant query's filter, or every read becomes a scatter-gather across all partitions, and it must distribute traffic evenly. A high-cardinality key with a skewed access distribution produces a hot partition that saturates while the rest idle.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Walk the learner through three candidate keys for one table, tabulating for each which queries become single-partition, which become scatter-gather, and where the hot key is. The exercise ends with the realistic conclusion that no key serves every pattern, so some queries must move to a separate read model.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Failover is automatic, so replication is also our backup strategy.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Replication faithfully reproduces every operation, including a DELETE with a missing WHERE clause and including corruption, and it arrives on every replica within milliseconds. Backups defend against a different failure class: human error, application bugs, and corruption.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Ask the learner to describe, step by step, what their replicas contain 200 milliseconds after an accidental mass delete. Then require a point-in-time backup plan with storage isolated from the primary's credentials and a scheduled restore drill, on the grounds that an untested backup is a belief rather than a backup.

competencies.title: Transactional versus analytical workloads and data movement
competencies.description: Distinguish OLTP from OLAP and search workloads, and design the movement between them: change data capture, transactional outbox, derived read models, search indexes, and the freshness and cost tradeoffs each implies.

desiredOutcomes.description: Design an outbox- or CDC-driven pipeline to a search index or read model and justify it over dual writes.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner writes the event inside the business transaction, identifies the resulting at-least-once delivery, and states the idempotency obligation it places on the consumer.

desiredOutcomes.description: Separate an analytical workload from the transactional store and state the accepted freshness as a number.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner names both damage mechanisms (buffer pool eviction and version retention) and writes a freshness statement a non-engineer would understand.

desiredOutcomes.description: Distinguish a read model from a cache and specify its rebuild procedure.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner explains that a read model is a derived authoritative artefact with its own backfill, rebuild, and correctness monitoring, and can state how long a full rebuild would take.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: It's only one report a month — just run it against production.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The analytical scan evicts the transactional hot working set from the buffer pool, so ordinary point lookups start going to disk for the duration and beyond. Separately, a long-running query blocks version cleanup. The report damages the transactional workload far more than the reverse.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner run an aggregation against a loaded transactional table and record point-lookup latency and buffer hit ratio before, during, and after. Require both mechanisms — eviction and version retention — in the written explanation, since learners reliably find only the first.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: We write to the database and then to the search index, so they stay in sync.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: There is no transaction spanning two systems. When the second write fails the two disagree permanently, with nothing to roll back, no error surfaced to the user whose request succeeded, and no detection. The defining property is that it fails silently and is discovered weeks later by a customer.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner implement the dual write, force the second call to fail, and then answer how an operator would detect the divergence and how long it would persist. The absence of any answer is the lesson. Then implement the outbox in the same transaction and compare.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A denormalized read model is basically a caching trick.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A cache is a copy you can discard and repopulate from the source on demand. A read model is a derived authoritative artefact with its own pipeline, rebuild procedure, backfill story, and correctness monitoring. If you cannot say how you would rebuild it from scratch and how long that takes, you have an unrecoverable divergence waiting to happen.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Ask the learner to delete their read model and rebuild it, timing the operation and verifying correctness against the source. Teams that cannot complete this exercise have discovered the distinction the hard way, in a rehearsal rather than an incident.

competencies.title: State placement, caching, and consistency
competencies.description: Decide where state lives (client, edge, shared cache, database), design cache keys, TTLs, and invalidation including stampede protection, and reason explicitly about staleness and what the user sees inside the window.

desiredOutcomes.description: Place each piece of state at the correct tier with the accepted staleness stated in plain language.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner produces a tiering table with tier, TTL, key structure, invalidation trigger, and a staleness statement a product manager could agree to.

desiredOutcomes.description: Design a cache key, TTL, and invalidation strategy including stampede protection.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner's key includes every input that varies the output, and the miss path is designed with single-flight, stale-while-revalidate, jitter, or proactive refresh.

desiredOutcomes.description: Design a UX-safe mitigation for a stated eventual-consistency window.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner applies the principle that a user always sees their own actions immediately and selects optimistic UI, read-your-own-writes routing, or displayed freshness appropriately.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Caching is an optimization you add at the end when something is slow.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Cache placement changes what different users see and how long a correction takes to reach them, which are correctness and product decisions rather than tuning knobs. Choosing a 60-second edge TTL for an article decides how long a retracted statement stays visible.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner build the tiering table before writing any caching code, with the staleness column filled in words a non-engineer would agree to. Then show a cache key missing an input serving one user's entitlement to another, which reframes caching as a security-relevant design decision.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Cache invalidation just means deleting the key.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The hard parts are who deletes it and whether they know to, how many tiers hold a copy, and what happens on the resulting miss under concurrency. Purge is a distributed operation that can partially fail, which is why short TTLs at outer tiers are often worth more than perfect invalidation logic.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner drive 2,000 requests per second at a 30-second-TTL key and count database queries per second across the expiry boundary. The spike of hundreds of queries in one second is the lesson; then implement single-flight and stale-while-revalidate and re-measure.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Eventual consistency means the data is sometimes just wrong.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: It means copies converge after a bounded delay. The data is from a moment ago, not incorrect. The engineering task is to bound the window and design what the user sees inside it, which is a UX decision rather than an unavoidable defect.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Introduce a deliberate three-second delay between a write and its appearance in a cached list, have the learner experience the resulting double-submit, then implement both optimistic UI and read-your-own-writes routing. Anchor with the rule that a user always sees their own actions immediately while other people's may be delayed.

competencies.title: Authentication, authorization, and trust boundaries
competencies.description: Distinguish authentication from authorization, implement session and token-based schemes with their revocation tradeoffs, place authorization checks at the resource, and identify trust boundaries, secret handling, and common server-side vulnerability classes.

desiredOutcomes.description: Select a credential mechanism from the revocation requirement, cross-service topology, and scaling pressure, in that order.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner justifies the choice against the revocation requirement first and names the condition that would flip the decision.

desiredOutcomes.description: Enforce authorization at the resource and demonstrate why client-side or gateway-only enforcement is insufficient.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner writes a check that compares the resource's owner and state to the caller after fetching it, and returns 404 where existence is sensitive.

desiredOutcomes.description: Conduct a threat-boundary review identifying an authorization gap and a secret-handling defect.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner produces a boundary map including inbound webhooks and CI/CD, an endpoint-level authorization table, and an explicit accepted-risk list with owners.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: JWTs are more secure than sessions.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: They trade server-side revocation for statelessness, and revocation is the property that matters most during an incident. Statelessness is a scaling property, not a security one. Short-lived access tokens plus a checked refresh token are effectively a session with a bounded window of unrevocability.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Give the learner a stated legal obligation to terminate access within minutes and ask them to satisfy it with 12-hour JWTs. Working through the options — revocation list, key rotation, short-lived tokens — makes them state the trade explicitly rather than inheriting it.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The frontend hides the admin button, so that action is protected.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The client is untrusted input. Anyone can issue the request the button would have issued. Worse, the common partial fix — checking the caller's role — authorizes the action type rather than the specific resource, which is how any manager ends up able to read any venue's data.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner log in as customer A and use curl with A's own cookie to request customer B's record by ID. Getting data back is the demonstration. Then require the fix to compare the resource's owner to the caller after fetching, and to return 404 rather than 403 where existence is sensitive.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Validation happens at the edge, so internal services can trust their input.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Trust is a property of a boundary defined by what can actually reach a component, not by the arrows on an architecture diagram. A misconfigured network rule, a compromised sibling service, a developer's port-forward, or a future service all bypass the gateway.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner draw every path that can reach an internal service, explicitly including inbound third-party webhooks and CI/CD, then attempt a direct call bypassing the gateway. Require per-service caller authentication or a written accepted risk with an owner and revisit date.

competencies.title: Service decomposition and inter-service communication
competencies.description: Evaluate monolith, modular monolith, and multi-service topologies; define boundaries by coupling, change cadence, and data ownership; and choose between synchronous calls and asynchronous messaging per interaction.

desiredOutcomes.description: Recommend a topology from team size, change cadence, and coupling, and name the largest cost accepted.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner identifies whether the pain is organisational, checks for a cheaper non-architectural fix first, and names the modular monolith where appropriate.

desiredOutcomes.description: Draw boundaries by business capability and defend them against a layer-based split.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner traces one feature through both splits counting hops, applies the change-cadence, data-ownership, and transactional tests, and names the distributed monolith outcome.

desiredOutcomes.description: Choose synchronous or asynchronous per interaction with the required guarantees stated.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner asks whether the caller needs the answer to proceed, computes the availability chain cost of each synchronous call, and specifies delivery and ordering guarantees for async ones.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Microservices are the mature, correct architecture to aim for.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The benefits are almost entirely organisational: independent deployment, independent scaling, team autonomy. A small team has no organisational problem for them to solve and pays the full distributed cost — tracing, sagas, partial failure, deployment orchestration — for a benefit it cannot use.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner write the topology decision for three staffing scenarios (4 engineers pre-launch, 15 in three teams with painful deploys, 90 in twelve teams) and state the trigger for each. Introduce the modular monolith explicitly, since learners who have never seen it treat the choice as binary.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Services should be split by technical layer — an auth service, a database service, a validation service.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: That maximises cross-service chatter per feature: one user action crosses every service, so nothing can be deployed independently and every schema change touches five codebases in a coordinated sequence. This is the distributed monolith — all the cost of distribution, none of the benefit.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Make the learner trace a single feature through the layer-based split and count the network hops, then repeat with a capability-based split and count again. The hop count is the argument. Follow with the three boundary tests: change cadence, exclusive data ownership, and transactional need.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Async just means I don't await the response.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Dropping the await gives you a lost request, not a decoupled interaction: no durability, no retry, no visibility, and failures become invisible rather than isolated. Real asynchronous messaging needs a durable intermediary plus decisions about delivery semantics, ordering, dead-lettering, and acceptable lag.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner call a service without awaiting, kill the process mid-flight, and try to determine afterwards whether the message was delivered. The impossibility of answering is the point. Then rebuild it on the outbox and enumerate the four required decisions.

competencies.title: Designing for partial failure
competencies.description: Apply timeouts, bounded retries with jittered backoff, idempotency keys, circuit breaking, bulkheads, backpressure, and graceful degradation; reason about failure domains and blast radius.

desiredOutcomes.description: Make a cross-service write safe to repeat under an ambiguous timeout.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner applies the full pattern — timeout, bounded jittered retry, stable idempotency key, circuit breaker, bulkhead — and can name the distinct failure each component addresses.

desiredOutcomes.description: Identify failure domains and design a graceful-degradation path preserving core function.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner produces a dependency-by-dependency degradation table, identifies the true single point of failure, and flags which degradation choices are business rather than engineering decisions.

desiredOutcomes.description: Quantify the availability cost of a synchronous dependency chain and reduce it.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner multiplies the chain, identifies which calls are non-essential, and demonstrates the availability gain from converting them to asynchronous.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Retrying makes the system more reliable.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Without idempotency, retries duplicate side effects — double charges, double orders. Without bounded attempts and jittered backoff, synchronised retries against a struggling service convert a brownout into an outage and prevent recovery. Retries and idempotency keys ship together or not at all.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner add a retry to a payment call with no idempotency key, force a timeout on a request that actually succeeded, and observe the double charge. Then add a stable key generated once per logical operation and re-run the same test.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If the happy path works, edge cases are rare enough to ignore.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: At ten million requests a day a one-in-a-million failure happens ten times daily, and a dependency at 99.9% availability is down 43 minutes a month on a schedule you do not control. The tail is the workload, so designing only the happy path leaves most real traffic undesigned.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner compute, from their own traffic figures, how many times per day a one-in-a-million event occurs and how many minutes per month each dependency is expected to be unavailable. Converting rarity into a count per day is what changes the intuition.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Failure means the request returned an error.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A clean error is the good case: you know nothing happened. The dangerous case is the timeout, where the caller cannot tell whether the work was performed. Treating timeouts as non-events causes both silent duplicate work and wrongly dropped operations.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Construct the exact scenario: the downstream call succeeds but responds after the caller's timeout. Have the learner predict what happens on retry, observe the duplicate, and then resolve it with an idempotency key so the ambiguity is handled rather than assumed away.

competencies.title: Capacity estimation and scaling tradeoffs
competencies.description: Estimate load, storage, and cost from product requirements; identify the binding bottleneck; and choose among vertical scaling, horizontal replication, partitioning, caching, and queue-based load levelling.

desiredOutcomes.description: Produce a capacity estimate from product numbers and name the binding bottleneck.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner computes peak request rate, write rate, and total storage after retention, then identifies the highest-utilisation resource and proposes changes only against it.

desiredOutcomes.description: Reject a premature scaling proposal with arithmetic rather than opinion.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner shows the numbers, states the conclusion explicitly, and names at least two concrete costs the premature change would have imposed.

desiredOutcomes.description: Distinguish capacity problems from availability problems and select the matching remedy.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner recognises when a system is failing because dependencies are down rather than because it is overloaded, and does not propose replication as a remedy.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Scaling means adding more servers.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: When the bottleneck is a shared singleton — one primary database, one lock, one queue, one third-party dependency — replication past that point adds contention rather than capacity, and can make things worse by increasing pressure on the saturated resource.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Give the learner a system where all instances share one database that is the constraint, have them add instances, and measure that throughput does not improve. Then require that every scaling proposal in the course name the target resource and its current utilisation first.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Design for the peak we might hit someday.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Premature scale-out costs money and velocity, and irreversible choices like a partition key permanently constrain the system in exchange for capacity that is never used. The discipline is estimating the actual order of magnitude before choosing.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner do the arithmetic on a realistic product before proposing anything: the totals are usually one or two orders of magnitude below intuition. Then have them write down what a premature sharding decision would have cost in engineering months and in query flexibility.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Sharding is a scaling technique we can add later if we need it.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The partition key constrains data modelling and query shape retroactively. Adding partitioning to an existing system means re-examining every query for whether it still routes, rewriting those that do not, and physically redistributing all data. It belongs in a design review, not an implementation ticket.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner choose a partition key for an existing schema and then audit every query they have already written against it, marking each single-partition or scatter-gather. The proportion that breaks is the argument that this is not a later decision.

competencies.title: Concurrency control and distributed coordination
competencies.description: Identify race conditions across processes and machines and select the right control: optimistic concurrency, pessimistic locking, atomic primitives, leases, fenced distributed locks, and leader election — including when coordination can be designed away entirely.

desiredOutcomes.description: Locate races in a multi-instance workflow and classify each as optimistic, pessimistic, or ownership-partitioned.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner applies the three-step procedure starting with whether ownership can be partitioned to eliminate the race entirely.

desiredOutcomes.description: Implement optimistic concurrency with version or ETag detection and define client-visible conflict resolution.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner uses a single conditional update rather than a read-then-write, returns 412 with the current value, and rejects blind automatic retry.

desiredOutcomes.description: Explain why a lease-based distributed lock requires fencing tokens and demonstrate the failure prevented.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner shows a paused holder writing after lease expiry and places enforcement at the resource, not the lock service.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A distributed lock gives me mutual exclusion.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A process can pause — garbage collection, VM migration, container throttling — past its lease expiry without knowing any time has passed, so two holders can both believe they hold the lock. Only a monotonically increasing fencing token, checked by the resource being written, rejects the stale writer.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner acquire a five-second lease, sleep eight seconds inside the critical section, start a second instance during the sleep, and observe both writes land. Then add fencing at the resource and repeat. Emphasise that the lock service cannot help because it is not present when the write happens.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Two servers won't realistically hit the same row in the same millisecond.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: At any real request rate collisions are continuous, and scheduled jobs on multiple instances start at exactly the same second by design. Improbability is not a correctness argument, and at scale the event is not even improbable.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Run twenty concurrent booking requests against three instances with no concurrency control and have the learner count the oversells. Seeing the failure happen immediately, without contrivance, removes the intuition faster than any explanation.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Coordination is the solution to concurrency.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Partitioning ownership so only one actor ever touches an entity removes the need to coordinate at all, and scales linearly where locking contends. Idempotency and commutative operations similarly eliminate rather than manage conflicts. Reaching for a lock first usually means skipping the cheaper question.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Require the learner to answer 'can one actor own this entity?' before proposing any lock, and to measure throughput for the partitioned design against the locked one. The scaling difference is the argument.

competencies.title: Consistency models, ordering, and consensus
competencies.description: Reason precisely about consistency guarantees — linearizable, causal, read-your-writes, monotonic reads, eventual — plus quorums, CAP and PACELC, cross-node ordering and clock problems, and where consensus protocols are and are not warranted.

desiredOutcomes.description: Select the weakest consistency model that satisfies a stated user-facing requirement and justify it against a stronger one.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner assigns models per operation rather than per system and can name a case needing a specific weak guarantee such as monotonic reads.

desiredOutcomes.description: Analyse a quorum configuration for its guarantees and partition behaviour using CAP and PACELC.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner applies R + W > N strictly, and explains the else-branch latency cost that applies when there is no partition.

desiredOutcomes.description: Identify the operations that genuinely require consensus and argue why the rest do not.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner recognises leader election and cluster membership as consensus problems and explains the establish-an-owner-then-decide-locally pattern.

desiredOutcomes.description: Explain why wall-clock timestamps cannot order cross-node events and apply a correct mechanism.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner cites skew and non-monotonic NTP corrections and selects a single sequencer, database sequence, logical clock, or consensus log.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: CAP says you pick two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Partitions are not optional — networks partition whether or not you choose it. The real choice is availability versus consistency during a partition, and PACELC adds the choice that applies the rest of the time: latency versus consistency, which is where you actually live.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner state, for two of their own datastores, what happens during a partition and what latency they pay for consistency when there is no partition. The else-branch is the one that surprises people, because it applies 99.9% of the time.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Timestamps order events across servers.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Wall clocks skew by tens of milliseconds even with NTP, and NTP corrections can move a clock backwards, so timestamps are neither comparable across machines nor reliably monotonic on one. Sorting by them produces wrong order and, where order decides outcomes, wrong results.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner sort events emitted by three servers by timestamp and compare against the true causal order recorded independently. Then have them route events for one entity through a single owner and use its sequence, which is the practical answer for most systems.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Anything important needs strong consistency.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The guarantee is per-operation. Most systems need linearizability at one or two chokepoints and are correctly served by read-your-own-writes, monotonic reads, or eventual consistency everywhere else. Blanket strong consistency multiplies latency, reduces availability, and buys nothing for most operations.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner tabulate six operations from one system and assign the weakest sufficient model to each. Typically exactly one is linearizable, and discovering that ratio for themselves is what generalises.

competencies.title: Event-driven and asynchronous processing
competencies.description: Design queue- and log-based systems: delivery semantics, partition keys and ordering, idempotent consumers, the transactional outbox, sagas and compensating actions, dead-letter handling, consumer lag, and replay and backfill.

desiredOutcomes.description: Design an at-least-once consumer with idempotent effects, an ordering-preserving partition key, and a dead-letter path.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner places the dedup insert and the effect in the same transaction, keys by the entity whose order matters, and keeps the partition moving past a poison message.

desiredOutcomes.description: Model a multi-service business transaction as a saga with explicit compensating actions.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner writes a compensation per step, orders the hardest-to-compensate step last, makes compensations idempotent, and stores saga state durably.

desiredOutcomes.description: Define consumer-lag alerting and a replay or backfill procedure.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner selects a leading indicator over an absolute threshold, ties an alert to time-to-retention, and gates downstream side effects during replay.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Exactly-once delivery is a feature you turn on.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The network cannot provide it: a sender cannot distinguish a lost message from a lost acknowledgement, so it must either retry and risk duplicates or not retry and risk loss. What is achievable is exactly-once processing — at-least-once delivery plus idempotent or transactional effects.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner kill a publisher between publishing and marking sent, restart it, and observe the duplicate. Then require an idempotent consumer with the dedup insert inside the same transaction as the effect, and demonstrate the bug that occurs when they are in separate transactions.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Queues absorb load, so it's fine if the consumer is a bit slow.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Lag compounds. A consumer 4% slower than arrival accumulates a backlog without bound, and once the oldest unprocessed message reaches the retention limit, messages are deleted before ever being processed — permanent, unrecoverable loss that produces no error at all.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner run a consumer at 96% of arrival rate and plot lag, then compute time-to-retention. Require an alert on processing-rate versus arrival-rate ratio rather than absolute lag, since the absolute threshold only fires once recovery is already expensive.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A saga is basically a distributed transaction.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: There is no rollback: every step already committed in its own service. Recovery runs forward through compensating actions that semantically undo the effect, and those are often harder than the original — refunding costs money, can fail, and takes days. Compensation is a design activity, not an error handler.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner write a compensating action for every step of a five-step saga and identify which is hardest, then reorder so that step is last. Realising that a single reordering eliminates most compensation work is the durable lesson.

competencies.title: Observability and operational practice
competencies.description: Instrument systems with structured logs, metrics, and distributed traces; define SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets; and operate change safely through canaries, feature flags, fast rollback, and incident diagnosis under time pressure.

desiredOutcomes.description: Instrument a request path and localize an injected fault using all three signals.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner uses metrics to find where, traces to find which operation, and logs to find which slice of traffic, and can state why no single signal suffices.

desiredOutcomes.description: Define an SLO with its error budget computed and derive alerting and rollback policy from it.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner converts the target into minutes per month, alerts on burn rate at two severities, and constrains rollback time as a fraction of the budget.

desiredOutcomes.description: Choose metric labels that do not destroy the monitoring system.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner keeps high-cardinality identifiers out of metric labels and places them in logs and traces where they belong.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: We have logs, so we have observability.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Logs answer questions you anticipated well enough to log. Observability means answering questions you did not anticipate, during an incident, about a specific slice of traffic — which needs metrics to detect, traces to localize across services, and logs to identify the affected slice. They are not substitutes.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Run a fault-localization drill in which the learner is given an injected fault and must name which signal narrowed the search at each step. Discovering that logs alone give no starting point — because nothing told them to look — is what separates the three roles.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Monitor the servers: CPU, memory, and disk.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Resource dashboards say a machine is busy. A service at 12% CPU returning errors is an outage that shows as healthy, and a service at 90% CPU serving every request in 50ms is fine. SLIs must measure something a user actually experiences: success rate and latency on the endpoints that matter.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Show the learner a green resource dashboard beside a broken checkout and ask what would have detected it. Then require every service they instrument to carry rate, errors, duration distribution, and one saturation metric before any resource dashboard is built.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Alert on anything abnormal so we never miss anything.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Alert volume without an error-budget threshold produces fatigue, and fatigue is the actual cause of slow incident response. Threshold alerts also fail in both directions: they page on harmless deploy blips and miss slow sustained degradation that never crosses the line.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner convert a threshold alert into two burn-rate alerts at different windows and severities, then verify that a 30-second blip does not page while a persistent 0.5% error rate eventually does. Any alert that must be routinely silenced should be treated as evidence of the misconception.

competencies.title: Architecture evaluation and communication
competencies.description: Compare candidate designs against stated requirements and constraints, document tradeoffs as ADRs, and defend a design verbally under questioning in a design review or system design interview.

desiredOutcomes.description: Write an ADR capturing context, decision, rejected alternatives, consequences, and a revisit trigger.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner's ADR contains at least two seriously-considered rejected alternatives with reasons, and a revisit trigger stated as a checkable condition.

desiredOutcomes.description: Present a design under time pressure and adapt correctly to a changed requirement.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner elicits constraints before designing, estimates before proposing, and responds to a change by naming what breaks, the option space, and the cost — unprompted.

desiredOutcomes.description: Argue both sides of a contested design decision, including the case for the option they rejected.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Learner produces a defensible case for the alternative and names the fact that would change their recommendation.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: There's a right answer to a system design question.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The reference architecture in your head was designed for constraints that were not stated in the question. What is assessed is whether you elicit the constraints, make the tradeoff explicit, and update correctly when a constraint changes — not whether you can recall a diagram.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Give the learner the same design prompt twice with different stated constraints — 5 engineers versus 90, one region versus three — and require different answers with the deciding constraint named. Producing two defensible, different designs from one prompt is the lesson.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A design doc describes what we built.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: If that is all it does, the code is better documentation. The value is in the rejected alternatives and the constraints that decided the choice, because eighteen months later someone must be able to check whether those constraints still hold rather than preserving an expired decision or reversing it and rediscovering the reason painfully.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Require every ADR in the course to include a Rejected Alternatives section and a one-sentence Revisit Trigger, and reject ADRs without them. Then have the learner read an ADR written by someone else and state, from it alone, what would make the decision wrong today.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Senior engineers design; I just implement.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Architectural decisions are made continuously inside implementation, whether or not they are recorded. A cache TTL is a consistency decision, a partition key is a scaling decision, and a role check without an ownership check is an authorization decision. The only question is whether they are deliberate and visible or accidental and buried.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner write an ADR for a decision their own team made where the reasoning lives only in a chat thread, then circulate it and ask whether the reasoning was captured correctly. The response — a correction, a realisation it was never explicit, or agreement — makes their own decision-making authority visible to them.

sections.title: From Client to Server: The Request Lifecycle
sections.description: Rebuilds a front end engineer's intuitions into an accurate model of a concurrent, multi-tenant server process. Traces where latency actually accumulates, exposes the shared-state bug that every front end engineer writes in their first months of backend work, separates CPU-bound from I/O-bound work, and establishes statelessness as the precondition for horizontal replication. Teaching examples are drawn from commercial air travel; the transfer exercises move to a hospital pharmacy.

learningObjectives.description: Trace an HTTP request end-to-end through load balancer, process, handler, and I/O boundary, naming where latency and queuing accumulate at each of the six hops.
Predict the behaviour of shared module-level state under concurrent requests as an explicit interleaving timeline, and refactor it into request-scoped or externalized state.
Distinguish CPU-bound from I/O-bound handler work using the busy-or-idle test, and select the appropriate concurrency remedy for each, supported by demand-against-capacity arithmetic.
Explain why statelessness is a precondition for horizontal replication, and identify the specific failures that follow from pinning user state to an instance.

motivationHooks.prompt:
## Why this matters

You already write asynchronous code. You know what a `fetch` is, what a promise is, and why blocking the main thread makes a UI stutter. That is genuinely most of the conceptual machinery a server runs on — which is exactly the trap.

The one thing that does not carry over is **who the program is for**. Your front end code runs in a browser tab owned by one person. Stash something in a module-level variable and it belongs to them; close the tab and it disappears. Server code runs in a process serving hundreds of people at once, and it stays up for weeks. A module-level variable there is a shared object every user can see and every user can overwrite.

Almost every serious bug a front end engineer writes in their first six months of backend work descends from that single difference. This section makes the difference obvious rather than surprising, and gives you the vocabulary — queuing, service time, tail latency, statelessness — that every remaining section is built on.

**Commit to an answer before you begin.**

An endpoint currently responds in 40ms. Your team adds a feature that costs **60ms of pure computation** per request. Traffic does not change. Nothing else changes.

What is the new p99 latency?

Write your number down somewhere you'll see it again. Most engineers say about 100ms. The real answer, in the system this section is built around, was **4 seconds** — and the reason is not that the estimate was slightly off. It is that the estimate assumed the wrong model of what a server is.

Here is a bug you can write today, that passes every test you would think to run, that works perfectly on your machine, and that will hand one customer another customer's data in production:

```js
let currentUser = null;
```

That's it. That's the whole bug.

## Back to your number

You predicted a latency. Here is the arithmetic that settles it.

Four instances share 200 requests per second, so each handles 50. Each request now demands **60ms of exclusive, unshareable CPU**. That is 50 × 60ms = **3,000ms of CPU demanded per 1,000ms of wall clock** — **300% of one event loop's capacity**.

Above 100% utilisation a queue does not settle at a higher level. It grows for as long as traffic continues. So the answer was never "40ms plus 60ms." It was "however long the queue is when your request arrives," which climbs until requests time out.

If you predicted around 100ms, you were reasoning as though each request pays only for its own work — which is true in a browser tab, and false in a shared process. **That correction is this whole section.** The 400ms of database waiting in the same handler, by contrast, was never a problem and still isn't: waiting releases the loop, and computing does not.

sectionSummary.content:
## What you should now believe

**A server is a multi-tenant process, not your front end code without a DOM.** One process, many concurrent users, weeks of uptime. Every piece of mutable state needs an explicit owner, and "the module" is never a valid owner.

**Latency is queuing plus service time across six hops, not one.** The database query is one of them and frequently not the guilty one. Measure which hop before you fix anything — the remedies for hops ③, ⑤, and ⑥ have nothing in common.

**Waiting is shareable; computing is exclusive.** A single event loop can hold tens of thousands of I/O-bound requests, because those requests spend their lives waiting. It cannot run two CPU-bound tasks at once. This, not connection count, is the real ceiling.

**Above 100% utilisation, latency diverges rather than degrading.** It stops being a fixed penalty and becomes "however long the queue is," which grows without bound. Demand against capacity is arithmetic you can do in your head, and it is worth doing before you ship.

**Statelessness is what makes instances interchangeable, and interchangeability is what makes replication work.** Pin state to an instance and routine events — a deploy, an autoscale, one crash — become user-visible incidents.

You also now have a habit worth more than any of these: **when someone says "it's slow," ask which hop before proposing a fix.**
keyTakeaways: Any module-level mutable value read across an `await` boundary is a bug.
Latency = queuing delay + service time, summed across six hops.
The diagnostic question for any handler work: during this work, is the CPU busy or idle?
CPU demand per instance = requests/sec × CPU-ms per request, against 1,000ms per second of capacity.
State that must outlive a request goes outside the process — never in a module variable, and never behind sticky sessions.
A concurrency bug that passes sequential testing has told you nothing about its safety.
