learningExperiences.title: Where the Time Actually Goes

contentBlocks.content:
## What you'll be able to do after this

1. **Trace an HTTP request end to end** through load balancer, process, handler, and I/O boundary, naming where latency and queuing accumulate.
2. **Distinguish queuing delay from service time**, and explain why the difference decides which fix you reach for.

These map to the course competencies `server-runtime-model` and `scalability-capacity-tradeoffs`.

## Start somewhere concrete: an airport check-in hall

Walk into a check-in hall. There is a queue rope, a row of desks, and behind the desks a baggage system that swallows suitcases and takes its own sweet time.

- The **queue rope** is your load balancer. It decides which desk you go to.
- Each **desk** is an instance of your server.
- Each **agent** is a thread of execution.
- The **baggage system, the visa database, the seat-map system** are your I/O: the agent starts a request and then *waits*.

Now the important observation. If the agent stands there staring at the screen while the baggage tag prints, the desk serves one passenger at a time and the queue grows. Real agents don't do that — they take your passport, start the visa lookup, and while it spins they hand you a landing card and answer a question.

That is exactly what an event loop does. One agent, many passengers in flight, because the waiting parts don't consume the agent.

But suppose a passenger arrives whose ticket requires the agent to manually recompute a fare across twelve fare buckets, by hand, for ninety seconds. During those ninety seconds the agent can't do anything else. Every other passenger at that desk waits.

**Waiting is cheap and shareable. Computing is expensive and exclusive.** Hold onto that sentence; the rest of this section is consequences of it.

terms.definition: One running copy of your server program, with its own memory. Nothing in that memory is visible to another process.
One process running on one machine or container. Three instances means three separate copies with three separate memories.
A component in front of your instances that decides which instance receives each incoming request.
The full path of a single request: client, load balancer, instance, handler, I/O, and back. Latency accumulates at every hop, not just the database.
How long the work itself takes once it starts.
How long a request waits before its work starts, because the server was busy.
The latency of the slowest requests, quoted as p95 or p99. Averages hide it completely.
A fixed, reusable set of database connections shared by all requests on an instance. Size it with Little's Law, not with request concurrency.

contentBlocks.content:
## The six hops

Here is the full path, with the place where time accumulates named at each hop.

```
Browser
  │  ① network time (DNS, TLS, transit)
  ▼
Load balancer
  │  ② LB queuing — requests waiting for a free instance connection
  ▼
Instance (one process)
  │  ③ event-loop queuing — your callback waiting its turn
  ▼
Handler function
  │  ④ handler service time — parsing, validation, your logic
  ▼
Connection pool
  │  ⑤ pool wait — no free DB connection, request waits
  ▼
Database
  │  ⑥ query execution time
  ▼
  ... and back up the same path, adding serialization on the way out
```

A front end engineer's instinct, when told "the endpoint takes 3 seconds," is to blame ⑥. In practice ⑥ is often 8 milliseconds and the other 2,992 milliseconds are sitting in ③ and ⑤.

Why does that matter so much? Because **the fixes are completely different.** If ⑥ is slow you add an index. If ③ is slow you have CPU-bound work blocking the loop. If ⑤ is slow your pool is misconfigured or your queries hold connections too long. Fixing the wrong one costs you a week.

You will meet hop ⑤ properly in `s7-database-systems`, where you size it with arithmetic rather than intuition. For now, know it exists and that it queues.

contentBlocks.title: The one-line version
contentBlocks.content: **Latency = queuing delay + service time**, summed across six hops. Almost everyone reasons only about service time at hop ⑥, which is why almost everyone misdiagnoses their first serious latency incident.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Blaming the database before measuring it.** Latency is queuing plus service time across six hops. Instrument the query first; if it is fast, the answer is upstream of it.

**2. Reporting the mean instead of a percentile.** A mean of 80ms is consistent with everyone getting 80ms *or* with 5% of users getting 1.5 seconds. Only one of those is an outage, and the mean hides it.

**3. Reasoning about capacity without arithmetic.** Requests per second times CPU-milliseconds per request, against 1,000ms per second per loop. It takes ten seconds and it settles most arguments.

**4. Assuming added work adds proportional latency.** Below saturation it roughly does. Above 100% utilisation the queue never drains and latency diverges instead.

**5. Ignoring hop ⑤.** Connection-pool acquisition is invisible on most dashboards and is a frequent cause of tail latency. It gets sized properly in `s7-database-systems`.

**6. Treating the six hops as a checklist rather than a search.** The point is to eliminate hops quickly, not to inspect all of them.

interactionSequence.prompt: Before you read the worked example below — an endpoint currently takes 40ms. The team adds a loyalty-tier calculation that costs **60ms of pure CPU** per request. Nothing else changes. **Predict the new latency at p99**, and write one sentence explaining your reasoning. Commit to a number; you'll compare it against what actually happens.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Most people predict something near 100ms — the old latency plus the new work. That prediction assumes each request pays only for its own computation. Hold your number. The worked example computes what actually happens, and the gap between your prediction and the result is the single most useful thing in this experience.
hints: How many requests per second is one instance handling, and how much CPU does each now demand?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your predicted number?

interactionSequence.prompt: Put the six hops of a request's path into order, from the browser inward to the database.
options: Connection pool acquisition
Network time from the client
Handler service time
Query execution in the database
Load balancer queuing
Event-loop queuing inside the instance

optionFeedback.feedback: Pool acquisition is hop ⑤ — after your handler has begun and decided it needs the database. It is the hop most often invisible in dashboards and most often responsible for tail latency.
Network time is hop ①, before anything of yours runs. Server-side timing largely excludes it, which is why a slow client is rarely the explanation for a bad server-side p99.
Handler service time is hop ④ — your own parsing, validation, and logic. This is the only hop most people think about.
Query execution is hop ⑥, the last one. It is the hop most people blame first.
Load balancer queuing is hop ②, where requests wait for a free connection to any instance.
Event-loop queuing is hop ③ — your callback waiting its turn behind other work on the same instance. This is where CPU-bound handlers do their damage.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The order is: network → load balancer queuing → event-loop queuing → handler service time → pool wait → query execution. Two of these are pure queuing (② and ③), one is a hybrid (⑤), and only one is the database. When you next hear "the endpoint is slow," you now have five other candidates.
feedback.correctiveFeedback: Check the two hops you placed adjacent to the database. Pool acquisition happens *before* the query, not after — the request has to obtain a connection before it can ask anything.
hints: Work outside-in: what happens before any of your code runs at all?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: An endpoint's p99 latency is 3.2 seconds. Instrumentation shows the database query it runs completes in 11ms, consistently, on every call. What is the most useful next question?
options: How much CPU-bound work is in the handler, and how deep is the event-loop queue?
Which index is missing from the table the query reads?
Can we add more instances to spread the load?
Is the client's network connection slow?

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. With hop ⑥ ruled out by measurement, the remaining candidates are queuing at ③ or ⑤, both usually driven by CPU-bound work holding the loop.
The query already completes in 11ms, so it is not the bottleneck and an index changes nothing. This is the reflex that costs a week on the wrong layer.
Adding instances may eventually help, but proposing capacity before knowing what is saturated risks adding pressure to a shared dependency rather than relieving it.
Network time is hop ①, and a server-side p99 largely excludes it. A consistent 3.2 seconds across many clients points inside your system.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The discipline here is small but it is the whole competency: **measure which hop, then fix that hop.** You will do this for real with traces and saturation metrics in `s6-production-readiness-review`, but the reasoning is available to you now, with nothing but a stopwatch around the query.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: your prediction in the first question was probably around 100ms, and the real answer was measured in seconds. **Explain to a teammate, in two or three sentences, why adding 60ms of CPU work did not add 60ms of latency.** Use the words *demand* and *capacity*.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A strong answer says something like: each instance receives 50 requests per second, each now demanding 60ms of exclusive CPU, so demand is 3,000ms of CPU per 1,000ms of wall clock — 300% of capacity. Past 100% the queue never drains, so latency is not "old plus new," it is "however long the queue is when you arrive," which grows without bound. If your explanation didn't include the arithmetic, write it out once by hand; the numbers are what make this stick rather than the phrasing.
hints: How many milliseconds of CPU does one event loop have available per second?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you?

workedExamples.problem:
An airline's check-in API handles **200 requests per second across 4 instances**. Each request takes 40ms of handler time, mostly waiting on I/O. p99 latency is 90ms, and everyone is happy.

The airline adds a loyalty-tier calculation to the endpoint. It costs **60ms of pure CPU** per request. Nothing else changes. Engineering expects latency to rise from 90ms to roughly 150ms.

Observed result: **p99 goes to 4 seconds**, and some requests time out entirely. Explain why.
steps: **Step 1 — compute per-instance load.** 200 requests/sec ÷ 4 instances = **50 requests per second per instance**.
**Step 2 — compute CPU demand per instance.** Each request needs 60ms of exclusive, non-shareable CPU. 50 × 60ms = **3,000ms of CPU demanded per 1,000ms of wall clock**.
**Step 3 — compare against capacity.** One event loop provides **1,000ms of CPU per second**. Demand is 3,000ms. The instance is at **300% of capacity**.

**Step 4 — reason about the queue.** Above 100% utilisation, the queue at hop ③ does not stabilise at a higher level. It grows for as long as traffic continues. Latency is not a fixed penalty; it is however long the queue happens to be when your request arrives.

**Step 5 — check the hop you didn't blame.** The original 40ms of I/O-bound work was never the problem and still isn't. That work *released* the loop while it waited. Sixty milliseconds of computation broke what four hundred milliseconds of database waiting would not have.
workedExamples.conclusion: **When utilisation exceeds 100%, latency does not degrade proportionally — it diverges.** The generalisable rule is that I/O time and CPU time are not interchangeable units of "work." Adding 60ms of waiting to this endpoint would have been nearly free; adding 60ms of computing was fatal. Any time you are asked to predict the effect of new work, first ask which kind it is, then compute demand against 1,000ms per second per loop.

fadedVariant.problem: Same airline, different endpoint. A **baggage-tag PDF renderer** handles 90 requests per second across 6 instances. Each request costs **30ms of CPU** to render. Work out whether this endpoint is healthy, and by how much.
givenSteps: **Step 1 — per-instance load.** 90 requests/sec ÷ 6 instances = 15 requests per second per instance.
**Step 4 — interpret.** Compare your figure from step 3 against the 70% guideline that leaves headroom for traffic variance and garbage collection.
blankedStepPrompts: **Step 2 —** compute the CPU demand per instance, in milliseconds of CPU per second. Show the multiplication.
**Step 3 —** express that demand as a percentage of one event loop's capacity.
**Step 5 —** the airline expects traffic to triple next summer. State what happens then, and give the minimum instance count that keeps utilisation under 70%.
blankedStepAnswers: 15 requests/sec × 30ms = **450ms of CPU demanded per 1,000ms of wall clock**.
450ms ÷ 1,000ms = **45% utilisation**. The endpoint is healthy today, with real headroom — a queue forms only transiently and drains quickly.

At 3× traffic, per-instance demand becomes 45 × 30ms = 1,350ms per second, or **135% utilisation** — past saturation, so latency diverges exactly as in the worked example. To stay under 70%: total demand is 270 requests/sec × 30ms = 8,100ms of CPU per second, and 8,100 ÷ 700 gives **12 instances** (rounding up). Note that the honest alternative is to move the render off the request path entirely, which costs no instances at all.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Name the six places in a request's path where time accumulates, in order, from the browser to the database and back. For each, say in a few words what would cause time to be lost there.
A handler does 400ms of database waiting and 40ms of computation. Which of those two numbers determines how many concurrent requests one event loop can hold, and why?

learningExperiences.title: The Bug You Are About to Write

contentBlocks.content:
## What you'll be able to do after this

1. **Predict the behaviour of shared module-level state** under concurrent requests, as an explicit interleaving timeline.
2. **Refactor that state** into request-scoped or externalized state, and say which of the two a given piece of data needs.

These map to `server-runtime-model` and to the first rung of `state-caching-consistency`, which you will climb again in `s3-data-layer`, `s4-state-caching-identity`, and `s8-distributed-programming`.

## Code that looks completely normal

Here is a handler that would pass review on most front end teams.

contentBlocks.caption: The bug — do not ship this

contentBlocks.content:
In a browser this is fine. There is one user, and `currentPassenger` means "the passenger currently being handled."

On a server, it means "the passenger most recently handled by *anyone*." Those are different sentences, and the difference is the whole of this section.

rows: records Ben's check-in with Amara's seat
contentBlocks.caption: Two overlapping requests on one instance. Amara receives Ben's boarding pass.

contentBlocks.content:
This is not a rare race. At 50 requests per second per instance it happens constantly.

**Why the `await` is the culprit.** Every `await` is a point where your function pauses and the runtime is free to run someone else's code. Between the `await` and the resumption, any module-level variable can have been changed by another request. The rule that follows is exact and worth memorising:

> **Any module-level mutable value read across an `await` boundary is a bug.**

contentBlocks.caption: The fix: request-scoped state

contentBlocks.content:
`passenger` is a local variable inside the function. Each invocation gets its own. There is no sharing, so there is no race.

**What may legitimately live at module level?** Things that are read-only after startup, or that are internally designed for concurrent use: configuration objects, compiled regexes, logger instances, the database connection pool itself. The test is not "is it at the top of the file" but **"does a request mutate it, and does another request read it."**

**And what about state that genuinely must persist between requests** — a shopping cart, a rate-limit counter, a user's session? It cannot live in a module variable, because the next request from the same user may land on a different instance, and because a deploy wipes it. It has to go *outside* the process: into the database, or a shared cache. That is the whole subject of `s4-state-caching-identity`, and this is the moment the need for it becomes obvious.

terms.definition: Data belonging to one request, created and discarded within it. The safe place for per-user data.
Data declared outside any handler. Shared by every request that instance serves; a bug whenever it is mutable and read across an await.
Occupying the event loop or a thread with work that prevents any other task from progressing.
Making progress on many tasks in overlapping time windows. One event loop is highly concurrent.
Executing many tasks at literally the same instant. Requires multiple cores and multiple threads or processes.
The one place a fact is authoritative. Everything else is a copy.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Caching a value in a module variable "for performance."** `let cachedUser` at module scope is shared across every user of that instance. You have not built a cache; you have built a data leak between users.

**2. Treating `async` as "this runs in the background."** `async` does not create a thread. An `async` function that does 500ms of `JSON.parse` blocks the loop for 500ms exactly as a synchronous one would. **`await` releases the loop; computation never does.**

**3. Assuming a local test proves concurrency safety.** One developer clicking through a UI generates one request at a time — the exact condition under which this bug is invisible. Concurrency bugs need concurrent load to appear.

**4. Reading a module variable after an `await` and thinking "it's the same tick."** It isn't. `await` is a scheduling boundary.

**5. Reaching for sticky sessions to make module state work.** Covered in the next experience, and it is a trap.

interactionSequence.prompt: Before reading the timeline table above: this handler is deployed and serving 50 requests per second on one instance. **Write down what you expect to go wrong, and roughly how often.** Be specific about *which line* causes it.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The failure is not a crash and not an error — it is a wrong-but-plausible response, which is why it survives to production. The line that causes it is the assignment to a module-level variable; the line that *reveals* it is any read of that variable after a subsequent `await`. At 50 requests per second the overlap is continuous, so this is not an occasional glitch: it is a steady stream of passengers receiving each other's data.
hints: What happens between the moment `currentPassenger` is assigned and the moment it is next read?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A teammate declares `let lastResult = null;` at module scope, assigns it inside a handler after an `await`, then reads it two lines later after another `await`. They argue it is safe because each request runs its own copy of the function. What is the accurate response?
options: It is safe, because each function invocation has its own execution context.
It is safe in Node because the event loop is single-threaded, so nothing can interleave.
It is safe as long as it works under local testing.
It is unsafe: between the two awaits, another request on the same instance can overwrite `lastResult`.

optionFeedback.feedback: Each invocation does have its own *local* variables — but `lastResult` is not local. It lives in the module, and every invocation on that instance points at the same one.
Single-threaded means no two callbacks run *simultaneously*. It does not mean they cannot *interleave*, and every `await` hands control to other pending work.
Local testing is sequential by nature, which is the one condition under which this bug is guaranteed not to appear. Its absence there is evidence of nothing.
Correct. Any module-level mutable value read across an `await` boundary is a bug. The fix is to make it a local variable inside the handler.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Notice that two of the wrong answers are *true statements applied incorrectly*. Node really is single-threaded; functions really do have their own execution contexts. The error is in the inference, not the fact — which is why this misconception survives so long in otherwise strong engineers.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Your team wants a per-user rate-limit counter. A developer proposes `const counts = new Map()` at module scope, incremented on each request. Which failure is the one they have *not* thought of?
options: The `Map` will grow without bound, since entries are never evicted.
With four instances behind a load balancer, each counts only its own share of traffic, so a user limited to 100 requests per minute can actually make 400.
`Map` is not thread-safe and will corrupt under concurrent writes.
The counter resets whenever the process restarts or is redeployed.

optionFeedback.feedback: A real bug and worth fixing, but it is a memory problem rather than a correctness one, and most people spot it.

Correct, and this is the one people miss. The counter is *per-instance*, so the limit silently multiplies by the number of instances — and it gets weaker every time you scale out, which is precisely backwards.
This one is not true on a single-threaded event loop: there is no torn write. Reaching for thread-safety here indicates a mental model imported from a different runtime.
True and commonly spotted, but it is the second-most-important failure. A limit that resets on deploy is bad; a limit that is silently 4× too permissive at all times is worse.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Both the distribution failure and the restart failure are real, and a complete answer names both. The fix is the same for each: the counter must live in shared external state with atomic increment and expiry, so all instances read and write one authoritative value. You will build exactly this in `s4-state-caching-identity`.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words, and thinking about a codebase you actually work in: **name one piece of state in it that you now suspect is in the wrong place.** Say where it currently lives, where it should live (request-scoped, or externalized), and what would go wrong today if two users hit it at once. If you're confident there isn't one, say what you'd grep for to check.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Useful things to grep for: module-scope `let` or `var` declarations in any file that exports a handler; assignments to `this.something` on a singleton service object; any `Map`, `Set`, or array declared outside a function and mutated inside one. Most codebases have at least one, and it is frequently a cache someone added for performance. Keep whatever you found — you will revisit it in `s4-state-caching-identity` when you decide which tier it belongs at, and again in `s8-distributed-programming` when the same question appears across machines rather than across requests.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you?

workedExamples.problem: A team reports that roughly 2% of their `/checkout` responses contain the wrong customer's saved address. It is not reproducible locally. The handler reads a customer record into a module-scoped variable, calls a pricing service, then reads the variable again to build the response. Diagnose it and fix it properly — not just enough to make the symptom go away.
steps: **Step 1 — locate the scheduling boundaries.** Find every `await` between the assignment and the final read. Here there is one: the pricing-service call. That call is the window, and its duration is the width of the window.

**Step 2 — estimate the window.** The pricing call takes ~120ms at p50. The instance handles ~15 requests per second. So roughly 15 × 0.12 ≈ **1.8 other requests arrive inside the window**, each of which overwrites the shared variable. A 2% corruption rate is entirely consistent with this.

**Step 3 — explain the non-reproducibility.** Local testing issues one request at a time, so the window is always empty. The bug is invisible by construction in the environment where it would be cheapest to find.
**Step 4 — fix it.** Make the customer record a local `const` inside the handler. Each invocation now has its own binding, and there is nothing to overwrite.

**Step 5 — check for siblings, because there is almost always more than one.** Grep the codebase for module-scope `let` and `var` in files that export handlers. Audit each against the test: *does a request mutate it, and does another request read it?*

**Step 6 — prevent recurrence.** Add a load test to CI that fires N concurrent requests with distinct inputs and asserts each response matches its own input. This is the only kind of test that would have caught the original bug.
workedExamples.conclusion: **The corruption rate is a function of the width of the `await` window and the request rate**, which is why a slow dependency makes this class of bug dramatically worse and why it is invisible under sequential testing. The durable takeaway is step 6: a concurrency bug that no test can express will come back. Once you have written the concurrent-load test, you have converted an occasional mystery into a build failure.

retrievalPractice.prompt: State the one-sentence rule about module-level variables and `await`. Then explain *why* `await` specifically is the dangerous boundary, rather than any other line of code.
Contrast request-scoped state with externalized shared state. Give one piece of data that belongs in each, and state what breaks if you swap them.

learningExperiences.title: Two Kinds of Work, and Why Instances Must Be Interchangeable

contentBlocks.content:
## What you'll be able to do after this

1. **Distinguish CPU-bound from I/O-bound handler work** and select the appropriate concurrency remedy for each.
2. **Explain why statelessness is a precondition for horizontal replication**, with a concrete failure to point at.

These map to `server-runtime-model` and `scalability-capacity-tradeoffs`.

## The diagnostic question

There is exactly one question that classifies handler work: **during this work, is the CPU busy or idle?**

rows: DB query, HTTP call to another service, reading a file, waiting on a queue
password hashing, image or PDF generation, sorting 100k rows in memory, parsing a 20MB JSON payload, crypto signing
Near zero — the loop is released during the wait
Total — the loop is held for the full duration
Increase concurrency: more in-flight requests, larger connection pools
Get the work off the loop: worker threads, a worker process, a background job, or precomputation
What breaks if you scale it wrong
Everything on that instance queues behind it
contentBlocks.caption: The classification decides the remedy. Getting it wrong means applying an I/O fix to a CPU problem, which does nothing.

contentBlocks.content:
This is the correct answer to the belief that a single-threaded runtime cannot scale. **A single event loop can hold tens of thousands of concurrent I/O-bound requests**, because those requests spend their lives waiting rather than computing. What it cannot do is run two CPU-bound tasks at once. The constraint is *what kind of work is in the handler*, not *how many requests there are*.

Two remedies worth knowing by name:

- **Multiple processes per machine.** Running one process per CPU core gives you genuine parallelism across cores while each process keeps its simple single-loop model.
- **Offloading.** Some work shouldn't be in the request at all. If a check-in triggers a 2-second PDF boarding-pass render, the request should record the check-in, return, and let a background worker render the PDF. You will build exactly this in `s8-distributed-programming`.

## Statelessness, and why it comes first

**Horizontal replication** means: when demand grows, run more instances behind the load balancer. It is the cheapest, most elastic form of scaling, and it is how essentially all modern web systems handle growth.

It has one precondition. **Any instance must be able to serve any request.**

Why? Because the load balancer does not generally know or care which instance served your previous request. If instance #2 holds your shopping cart in memory and your next request lands on instance #5, your cart is gone. If instance #2 restarts during a deploy — which happens on *every* deploy — the cart is gone for everyone it was serving.

So statelessness is not an aesthetic preference. It is the property that makes instances **interchangeable**, and interchangeability is what makes replication work.

terms.definition: Work whose time is spent waiting on something external. The CPU is idle during the wait, so the wait is shareable.
Work whose time is spent computing. The CPU is busy throughout, so the time is exclusive and unshareable.
The single-threaded scheduler that runs your JavaScript one callback at a time and resumes callbacks when I/O completes.
A fixed set of OS threads that can each run code truly simultaneously.
The property that any instance can serve any request, because no instance holds information the others lack. The precondition for horizontal replication.
Adding capacity by running more instances rather than by making one instance bigger.
Load-balancer affinity pinning a user to one instance. Converts a replicable cluster into several fragile single-instance systems.
The one resource that limits the whole system. Everything else has slack, and proposals should target only this.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Scaling up instances to fix a saturated shared dependency.** If all instances share one database and the database is the bottleneck, adding instances adds *more* pressure to it. You must know where the bottleneck is before replication means anything — a theme that returns as a full competency in `s5-distributed-resilience`.

**2. Reaching for sticky sessions to keep state in memory.** See the worked example below. It looks like a fix and is a structural regression.

**3. Classifying by how long something takes rather than by what it does.** A 900ms database call is I/O-bound; a 90ms image resize is CPU-bound. The slow one is harmless and the fast one is dangerous.

**4. Sizing a connection pool by intuition.** A pool of 5 with 50 concurrent requests means 45 requests queue at hop ⑤. A pool of 500 may collapse your database. This gets computed properly in `s7-database-systems`.

**5. Assuming "more instances" is free.** Each one opens its own connections to every shared dependency. Ten instances with a pool of 50 is 500 connections against one database.

interactionSequence.prompt: Your service holds 8,000 concurrent long-polling connections on a single Node process with negligible CPU work per connection, and it is perfectly healthy. A colleague says the architecture is fundamentally limited because Node is single-threaded. What is the strongest correction?
options: Node is not actually single-threaded; it uses a thread pool for all operations.
Concurrency here comes from non-blocking I/O — 8,000 waiting connections consume almost no CPU — so the real limit is CPU-bound work in handlers, not connection count.
The colleague is right, and the service should be rewritten in a multi-threaded language before it grows.
The limit is real but can be ignored because you can always add more servers.

optionFeedback.feedback: Node maintains a small internal thread pool for a few filesystem and crypto operations, but your JavaScript runs on one thread. Overstating this gives you a false model that will mislead you later.
Correct, and it names the actual constraint. Waiting is shareable; computing is exclusive. This system is healthy precisely because it does almost no computing per connection.
The running system is empirical evidence against this. Eight thousand concurrent connections on one thread is exactly what a non-blocking runtime is good at.
This concedes a limit that does not exist as stated, and treats added servers as a universal remedy — which fails whenever the bottleneck is a shared resource rather than per-instance capacity.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Keep the shape of this argument. You will use it again in `s5-distributed-resilience` when someone proposes adding capacity to fix an availability problem, and in `s7-database-systems` when someone proposes a larger connection pool to fix a saturated database. In all three cases the move is the same: **name the resource that is actually saturated before proposing anything.**

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A team stores in-progress checkout state in instance memory and enables sticky sessions to make it work. Which consequence is the *most architecturally significant*?
options: Memory usage per instance grows with the number of active users.
Debugging is harder because you must find which instance holds a given session.
Instances stop being interchangeable, so every deploy and every instance failure destroys live user state, and load can no longer be distributed evenly.
It violates REST's statelessness constraint, which is a specification compliance issue.

optionFeedback.feedback: True but secondary — a capacity concern with straightforward remedies, and not what makes the design structurally fragile.
True but secondary. An operational annoyance rather than the thing that causes user-visible outages.
Correct. Interchangeability is the precondition for horizontal replication, so losing it converts routine, expected events — deploys, autoscaling, a single crash — into user-visible incidents.
Wrong emphasis. The problem is not that a specification is displeased; it is that the system now fails during ordinary operations. Reason from failure modes, not from conformance.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The tell for this class of decision is that it works fine in staging and fails on your first busy deploy. Whenever a design requires the load balancer to remember something about a user, ask what happens during a deploy — that single question surfaces the problem before it ships.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt:
Two engineers propose fixes for an endpoint whose p99 has degraded badly after a new feature added server-side PDF generation.

**Engineer A:** "Increase the connection pool from 10 to 100 and add two more instances. We're clearly resource-starved."

**Engineer B:** "Move the PDF render to a background worker and return a job ID. The endpoint records the request and responds immediately."

**Which is right, and — more importantly — what single measurement would settle it before anyone writes code?**

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Engineer B is right, but the reason matters more than the verdict. PDF generation is CPU-bound, so it holds the event loop for its full duration and no amount of connection-pool capacity helps — those connections would sit idle while the loop is busy. Engineer A's fix targets hop ⑤ when the problem is at hop ③.

The measurement that settles it: **event-loop lag** (or equivalently, CPU utilisation of the process) during the slow window. If the loop is saturated, it is CPU-bound and only offloading helps. If the loop is idle while requests queue for connections, Engineer A is right after all. One metric, one decision — and it takes minutes to collect.

Note that Engineer A's instinct is not stupid; it is the correct fix for a *different* problem. The skill being built here is telling the two apart before spending a sprint.
hints: During a PDF render, is the CPU busy or idle?
Which hop does a larger connection pool affect?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

workedExamples.problem: An airline stores each passenger's in-progress booking in instance memory. To make it work, they configure the load balancer for **session affinity** — once you hit instance #3, you always return to instance #3. Evaluate this design.
steps: **Step 1 — does it work at all?** Yes, for a while. Bookings complete correctly, and the feature ships.

**Step 2 — what happens on deploy?** Deploys replace instances. Every in-progress booking on every instance is lost simultaneously. The team responds by deploying only at 3 a.m., which slows every other change the team wants to make.

**Step 3 — what happens under uneven load?** Affinity is usually by client IP or cookie hash. A corporate travel agency behind one IP sends 40% of traffic to instance #3 while #1, #2, and #4 idle. Adding instances does not help, because new instances receive no existing sessions.

**Step 4 — what happens when instance #3 dies?** Every passenger pinned to it loses their booking, while the other three instances are perfectly healthy. A single instance failure became a user-visible outage for a quarter of users.

**Step 5 — cost the alternative.** Moving the in-progress booking into a shared store — a database row, or a cache entry keyed by booking ID — costs roughly one lookup per request, on the order of a millisecond.
workedExamples.conclusion: **Sticky sessions convert a stateless, replicable system into four fragile single-instance systems that merely look like a cluster.** One millisecond per request buys back deploys at any hour, even load distribution, and tolerance of instance failure. The generalisable test: whenever a design requires the load balancer to remember something about a user, ask what happens during a deploy. You will make this decision properly, with a tiering table, in `s4-state-caching-identity`; recognise the shape of it now.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Why must statelessness come *before* horizontal replication rather than after it? Give one concrete failure that occurs if you replicate a stateful service.
A handler makes a 900ms call to a payment provider. Another resizes an image in 90ms. Which one threatens the instance's ability to serve other requests, and why is it the faster one?

transferExercises.context: Hospital pharmacy — deliberately outside the air-travel domain used in the teaching examples, so the reasoning has to travel rather than the setting.
transferExercises.scenario:
A hospital pharmacy has **one pharmacist on duty**. Their work splits into two kinds.

**Verification:** sending a prescription to the drug-interaction database and waiting ~90 seconds for a response. The pharmacist does nothing during the wait.

**Compounding:** manually mixing a bespoke IV preparation. Twelve minutes of continuous, undivided attention.

The pharmacy handles 30 prescriptions per hour, of which 2 require compounding. Wait times have become unacceptable. Management proposes two options: **(a)** hire a second pharmacist, or **(b)** buy a faster interaction-database subscription that returns results in 20 seconds instead of 90.
transferExercises.task:
1. Classify verification and compounding using this section's vocabulary, justifying each with the diagnostic question from the comparison table.
2. Estimate the pharmacist-minutes per hour consumed by compounding alone. State what that implies about utilisation, showing the arithmetic.
3. Recommend (a) or (b), and explain in terms of **which resource is actually saturated**. State explicitly what the other option would and would not improve.
4. The manager also proposes: *"let's assign each ward its own dedicated pharmacist so they always deal with the same person — it'll be more efficient."* Name the server-side pattern this is equivalent to, and give two specific ways it will fail.
successCriteria: Verification classified as I/O-bound and compounding as CPU-bound, each justified by whether the pharmacist is occupied during the work rather than by how long it takes.
Compounding load computed as 2 × 12 = 24 minutes per hour, i.e. 40% of a single pharmacist's capacity, with the arithmetic shown.
Option (a) recommended, with the reasoning that the saturated resource is exclusive pharmacist attention, not database latency.
States that option (b) shortens a wait that costs the pharmacist nothing, so it improves per-prescription turnaround slightly but does not relieve the bottleneck.
Identifies the ward-dedication proposal as session affinity / sticky sessions.
Gives two concrete failures: uneven load between wards leaving one pharmacist idle while another is swamped, and total loss of service for a ward when its pharmacist is absent or on break.

transferExercises.context: Hospital pharmacy, continued — the shared-state failure transposed out of code entirely.
transferExercises.scenario:
The same pharmacy keeps **one clipboard** at the counter, labelled "Current Patient." The pharmacist writes the patient's name and allergy list on it when they begin, refers back to it when the interaction result arrives, and erases it when done.

On a busy afternoon, two prescriptions are in progress at once.
transferExercises.task:
1. Describe, as a concrete timeline of two overlapping prescriptions, exactly how this clipboard causes a patient to receive a drug they are allergic to. Lay it out as a table with a row per time step, in the same form as the two-request table in this section.
2. Identify the precise moment in your timeline that corresponds to an `await` in server code, and say why that moment specifically is the dangerous one.
3. Propose two different fixes — one analogous to request-scoped state, one analogous to externalized shared state — and say which situations call for each.
4. The pharmacy's incident review concludes: "this has never happened in eleven years of single-patient testing." Explain why that sentence is evidence of nothing.
successCriteria: Timeline shows the second prescription overwriting the clipboard while the first is still waiting on the interaction database, and the first pharmacist then reading the wrong allergy list.
Identifies the 90-second wait for the interaction result as the await-equivalent, and explains that it is dangerous because it is when other work gets a turn.
Request-scoped analogue given: one clipboard per prescription, carried with that prescription — nothing shared, so nothing to overwrite.
Externalized analogue given: allergy data read from the patient record at the point of use rather than transcribed, appropriate when the data must outlive the single interaction or be seen by others.
Explains that sequential single-patient operation is exactly the condition under which the failure cannot occur, so its absence carries no information about concurrent safety.

learningExperiences.title: Practical: Break It, Measure It, Fix It

contentBlocks.content:
## What you'll be able to do after this

Everything in this section, but with your own numbers rather than mine. Specifically: **induce both failures deliberately, measure them, fix them, and confirm the fix.** The numbers you record here get reused in `s6-production-readiness-review`, so write them down properly.

This is the first commit on **Meridian**, the venue booking platform you will build and refactor through all eight sections.

## Setup

Create a minimal HTTP server with three endpoints. Any runtime is fine; the instructions assume Node.

1. `GET /venues` — returns a hardcoded list after a simulated 30ms I/O wait (`await sleep(30)`).
2. `GET /venues/:id/report` — performs genuinely CPU-bound work: a **synchronous** loop computing a SHA-256 hash 200,000 times.
3. `POST /bookings` — deliberately written with the module-level-state bug.

contentBlocks.caption: Endpoint 3 — write it wrong on purpose

contentBlocks.content:
## Part A — the loop-blocking demonstration

1. Load-test `GET /venues` alone with **50 concurrent clients**. Record p50 and p99.
2. While that load is running, issue a **single** request to `/venues/:id/report`.
3. Record what happens to `/venues` p99 during that window.

**Write down:** how long was `/report` busy, and how many `/venues` requests were delayed by approximately that same amount? Explain the relationship in one sentence.

## Part B — the shared-state demonstration

1. Fire **20 concurrent** `POST /bookings` requests, each with a distinct customer name.
2. Count how many responses return a name that does not match the name that was sent.
3. Now run the same 20 requests **sequentially** and count again.

**Write down:** why does the sequential run pass, and what does that tell you about the value of your local manual testing?

## Part C — the fixes

1. Refactor `POST /bookings` to request-scoped state. Re-run Part B; confirm zero mismatches.
2. Move the `/report` computation into a worker thread or a separate process. Re-run Part A; confirm `/venues` p99 no longer spikes.

**Write down, in two sentences each:** which hop in the lifecycle diagram was responsible for each failure, and why the fix addresses that specific hop.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors in this lab
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Load-testing with a tool that issues requests sequentially.** If your client waits for each response before sending the next, you have reproduced your manual testing and will see nothing. Verify genuine concurrency before drawing conclusions.

**2. Using `await sleep()` for the CPU-bound endpoint.** A sleep releases the loop, which is the opposite of what you are trying to demonstrate. The hashing loop must be synchronous.

**3. Reporting the mean instead of p99.** The mean will barely move in Part A. The whole effect lives in the tail — which is the point.

**4. Declaring Part C successful after one clean run.** Concurrency bugs are probabilistic. Run the 20-request test at least five times before believing it.

**5. Skipping the write-downs.** They are the deliverable. The measurements are reused in `s6-production-readiness-review`, and the reasoning is what the assessment scores.

interactionSequence.prompt: Before running Part B: **how many of your 20 concurrent bookings do you predict will return the wrong customer name?** Give a number, not a range, and one sentence of reasoning. (There is no penalty for being wrong — the gap between your prediction and the result is the useful part.)

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Most people predict one or two. The actual figure is usually much higher — frequently the great majority of responses return the same one or two names, because every request that is inside the 50ms window when a later request overwrites the variable will read the later value. The width of the `await` window relative to the request arrival rate determines the corruption rate, exactly as in the diagnostic worked example. If your number was low, that instinct — "races are rare" — is the thing this lab exists to remove.
hints: How many of the 20 requests are inside the 50ms window at the same time?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that number?

interactionSequence.prompt: In Part A, you issued **one** request to `/report` and many `/venues` requests slowed down. What does this tell you about the relationship between a single CPU-bound request and the rest of the instance's traffic?
options: The CPU-bound request consumed a connection from the pool, leaving fewer for other requests.
One CPU-bound request holds the event loop for its full duration, so every other request on that instance queues behind it regardless of how cheap those requests are.
The operating system deprioritised the other requests because the CPU-bound one had higher load.
The `/venues` endpoint became slower because its own I/O wait increased under load.

optionFeedback.feedback: Neither endpoint touches a database in this lab, so no pool is involved. The coupling is through the loop, not through connections.
Correct. This is the defining property of CPU-bound work: it is exclusive. The other requests were not competing for a resource — they were simply not running at all.
The OS scheduler is not involved at this level. Within one process, one loop, the work is serialised by the runtime rather than by the kernel.
The simulated 30ms I/O wait is fixed and does not vary with load. The added latency is queuing at hop ③, not longer service time.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is the experiment that makes the loop concrete. One request, no shared database, no locks, no network contention — and the whole instance stalls. Keep the p99 numbers from before and after your worker-thread fix; they are the most persuasive artefact you will produce in this section, and you will want them again when you define SLOs in `s6-production-readiness-review`.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: You have now produced a bug that is **invisible under sequential testing and obvious under concurrent load**. Reflect: what does this imply about the tests currently protecting the code you work on? Name one test you could add this week that would catch this class of bug, and one reason your team might resist adding it.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The test is usually a small one: fire N concurrent requests with distinct inputs, assert each response matches its own input. It runs in seconds and needs no infrastructure. The common objections are that it is 'flaky' (it isn't — it is *probabilistic*, which is different, and you raise N until it is reliable) and that 'we'd have noticed in staging' (staging traffic is almost always sequential, so no). Bringing a measured before-and-after from this lab is what turns that conversation from an opinion into evidence — which is the pattern the whole course is training, and which becomes an explicit competency in `s6-production-readiness-review`.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you?

retrievalPractice.prompt: You fire 20 concurrent requests at a handler that writes to a module-level variable and reads it back after a 50ms await. Roughly what fraction return corrupted data, and what two quantities determine that fraction?

learningExperiences.title: Self-Guided: Instrument Something That Isn't Yours

contentBlocks.content:
## Why this one is different

Everything so far has been a system you could see inside. On your first day at any company with an existing codebase, you will be in the opposite position: something is slow, you did not write it, and you cannot read its source.

This exercise rehearses exactly that. You will reason about a system's internals **from the outside**, using nothing but response times — and then say honestly what additional measurement you would need to be sure.

The write-up is reused in `s6-production-readiness-review`. Keep it.

contentBlocks.title: Ground rules
contentBlocks.content: Pick a public API you are **allowed** to call politely. Read its terms of service first. Keep your request volume low and well-mannered — one request every 30 seconds is plenty. Identify yourself in a `User-Agent` header. Do not attempt to load-test someone else's service, do not probe for weaknesses, and stop immediately if asked to. The exercise is observation, not testing.

interactionSequence.prompt: After you have collected your data: **which hop do you believe is responsible for your widest p50-to-p99 gap, and what single additional measurement would let you rule out your second-best hypothesis?** Being specific about what you *cannot* determine from outside is the point of the exercise, not a shortcoming of it.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Strong answers usually land on one of four hypotheses and name what would separate them: **queuing** (would show as latency correlating with time-of-day traffic, and as a long right tail rather than a bimodal distribution), **a cold cache** (bimodal — a fast cluster and a slow cluster, with slow responses clustering after quiet periods), **a slow dependency** (latency correlating with a specific endpoint or parameter rather than with time), or **a CPU-bound path** (specific requests consistently slow regardless of load). From outside you can often distinguish these by varying *one* input at a time and by correlating with time of day — which is genuinely a lot. What you cannot see is the split between hops ③ and ⑤, and saying so precisely is a better answer than guessing confidently.
hints: Is the slowness spread across all requests, or concentrated in a distinct cluster?
Does it correlate with time of day, or with a particular parameter?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you?

selfGuidedExercise.objective: Reason about a real production system's internal behaviour from the outside, using only externally observable latency — the position you will occupy on your first day in any unfamiliar codebase.
selfGuidedExercise.realWorldContext: A public API you do not control and are permitted to call: a weather service, a transit-times API, a public library catalogue, a government open-data endpoint, or a hobby project's public API. Not a service you have an account with and not one you are testing on someone's behalf.
instructions: Choose a public API and **read its terms of service before sending anything**. Confirm that polite, low-volume automated access is permitted.
Write a script that calls one endpoint every 30 seconds and records the response latency and timestamp. Set a descriptive `User-Agent` that identifies you.
Let it run for **at least two hours**, ideally spanning a change in time of day.
Compute **p50, p95, and p99** — not the mean. The mean will hide exactly the behaviour you are learning to see.
Find the widest gap between p50 and p99 in your dataset, and note the time of day it occurred.

Write 200–300 words arguing for **one** explanation: queuing, a cold cache, a slow dependency, or a CPU-bound path. Say explicitly what additional measurement would let you distinguish it from your second-best hypothesis.
Save the write-up. You will return to it in `s6-production-readiness-review` and compare your outside-in reasoning against what real instrumentation would have told you.
materialsOrPrerequisites: Any HTTP client and a way to record timings — a shell script with curl is sufficient.
A way to compute percentiles: a spreadsheet, a few lines of Python, or a command-line tool.
A public API whose terms permit low-volume automated access.
reflectionPrompts: Did your latency distribution have one cluster or two? What does the shape alone tell you before you consider any other evidence?
Did the tail correlate with time of day? If so, what does that rule in — and what does it fail to rule out?
What is the single measurement you most wished you had, and which of the six hops would it have illuminated?
You now have a defensible hypothesis about a system you have never seen the source of. How does that change what you would say in your first week on an unfamiliar codebase?

verification.mode: self-assessment against criteria, with the write-up retained for use in the final section
selfAssessmentCriteria: I reported p50, p95, and p99 rather than the mean, and I can say why the mean would have been misleading here.
I collected at least two hours of data and can point to the specific time of my widest tail.
I committed to one explanation rather than listing all four as equally likely.
I named a specific additional measurement and said which hypothesis it would eliminate.
I was honest about what cannot be determined from outside the system, rather than overstating my confidence.
I respected the service's terms and kept my request volume low throughout.

sections.title: Designing the Contract
sections.description: Treats the API as a long-lived public interface with its own evolution and failure semantics — the one artefact you cannot refactor unilaterally. Covers resource modelling, actionable error taxonomies, pagination, idempotency as a contract obligation, style selection under stated constraints, breaking-versus-additive classification, expand/contract rollout, and the removal of storage leakage. Teaching examples come from parcel shipping and courier logistics; the transfer exercises move to municipal building permits.

learningObjectives.description: Model a set of product requirements as resources and operations with defined error, pagination, and idempotency semantics, specifying all six elements of a complete endpoint contract.
Justify a REST, RPC, or GraphQL choice against stated client and team constraints, naming the organisational cost of the recommendation unprompted.
Classify a proposed API change as breaking or additive using the correctly-written-existing-client test, and design a four-phase backward-compatible rollout for a breaking one.
Identify contract decisions that leak storage structure to clients and refactor to decouple them, using the would-a-database-change-force-an-API-change test.

motivationHooks.prompt:
## Why this matters

You have been on the receiving end of this your entire career. Every time an API returned `null` where you expected an array, every time a field silently changed type, every time you wrote a defensive `?.` chain because you didn't trust the payload — you were paying for someone else's contract decisions.

Now you make those decisions. And the asymmetry is brutal: **an API is the only part of your system you cannot refactor unilaterally.** You can rewrite your database layer on a Tuesday and nobody notices. Change a response field and you break every client, including the mobile app version from eight months ago that a customer has not updated and will not update.

So the contract is the one artefact you must get roughly right the first time, and must be able to evolve without breaking. This section comes *before* data modelling deliberately — because the most common architectural mistake is designing the database first and letting the API become a thin veneer over it, which welds your public interface to your storage decisions forever.

**Commit to an answer before you begin.**

Your API returns `"weight": 2.4` — kilograms, though the docs never said so. You now need to support pounds, so the field should become `{ "value": 2.4, "unit": "kg" }`.

There are **400 external integrators**, most of whom you have never spoken to.

How do you ship it? Write down your plan in one line.

Most engineers reach for `/v2`. That answer costs years of duplicated maintenance surface for a change to one field — and there is a route that ships the same change with no version bump at all.

There is one sentence you can put in your API documentation on day one — costing nothing, taking ten seconds to write — that converts an entire category of future changes from *breaking* to *additive*, permanently.

Most APIs don't have it. It appears in this section.

## Back to your plan

The route with no version bump is **expand/contract**, in four phases:

1. **Expand.** Add `mass: { value, unit }` *alongside* `weight`. Change nothing about `weight`. This is purely additive, so it ships immediately and breaks nobody.
2. **Announce and instrument.** Deprecate `weight` with a date — and **measure which clients still read it.**
3. **Migrate.** Contact the highest-volume consumers directly. Release notes reach the wrong people.
4. **Contract.** Remove `weight` once measured usage is near zero.

If you wrote `/v2`, notice what it would have cost: every endpoint duplicated forever, including the forty you didn't change, maintained for years because one 2019 integration will never migrate.

And if you wrote something like phases 1, 3, and 4 but skipped phase 2 — that is the more interesting near-miss, and the more common one. **Without measurement, "can we remove it now?" is unanswerable**, so the answer is always no, the deprecated field lives forever, and you pay the dual-maintenance cost you were trying to avoid. Phase 2 gets cut precisely because it is the only phase with no visible output.

sectionSummary.content:
## What you should now believe

**A contract is defined by what clients can rely on, not by what your code currently returns.** Undocumented behaviour that clients depend on is contract. Error message strings are contract the moment a client string-matches them.

**A complete endpoint specifies six things**, not three: resource, verb, success shape, actionable error taxonomy, collection traversal, and retry semantics. The three that get skipped don't go undecided — they get decided accidentally, one client at a time.

**Idempotency is a contract with two parties, and the client's half fails silently.** Only the caller knows two requests are the same logical operation, so the key must be generated once per operation and the obligation must be written down.

**There is no best API style, only constraints.** Who are the consumers, how many, can you coordinate their deploys, where is the pain today. GraphQL relocates design work into schema, resolvers, and per-field authorization rather than removing it.

**Versioning is what you do when expand/contract has failed.** Add alongside, announce and measure, migrate, remove. Phase two is the one teams skip and the one that makes phase four possible.

**The API describes the domain; the schema describes the storage.** They may resemble each other. They must be able to diverge — which in practice means an explicit mapping layer that feels like boilerplate for two years and then saves you.
keyTakeaways: The breaking-change test: could a correctly-written existing client, which you cannot update, fail because of this?
Write the tolerant-reader clause on day one — it converts a whole category of future changes to additive for free.
The idempotency key is generated once per logical operation by the client, never per attempt, and never by the server.
Use 409 when the request was well-formed but the state made it invalid; 400 when it was never valid.
Make cursors opaque. The moment clients can decode them, your sort key and partition strategy are frozen.
The leakage test: if we changed our database tomorrow, would this part of the API have to change?
Expand without a scheduled contract is not a migration — it is a permanent second field.
