**Find a modelling regret.** Look for a field that clearly means different things in different contexts, an entity that was obviously bolted on, or a place where the UI makes you do something twice because the model didn't anticipate it.
Write 400–600 words on the above.

**Then write one more paragraph — the important one.** Given the constraints the original team plausibly had (unknown product direction, small team, a deadline), argue that the decision you criticised was reasonable **at the time**. If you conclude it genuinely wasn't, say what they should have known and how.
Keep the write-up. You will use it in `s6-production-readiness-review`.
materialsOrPrerequisites: A product you use regularly and know well — familiarity matters more than the product.
Something to sketch entities and relationships on. Paper is fine.
No database access, no API keys, no account beyond your own.
reflectionPrompts: What is the product refusing to let you ask, and what would its schema need to look like for that question to be cheap?
Where did you find a stale count, and what does that tell you about their synchronization mechanism?
Is the regret you identified a modelling error, or a correct decision that a later product change invalidated? How would you tell the difference from outside?
Which of the six 'common errors' from this section can you see evidence of in a product built by professionals?

verification.mode: self-assessment against criteria, with the write-up retained for the design review in the final section
selfAssessmentCriteria: I sketched entities and cardinalities before consulting any documentation, so the inference is genuinely mine.
I identified something the product refuses to do and explained it in terms of a modelling or indexing constraint rather than assuming laziness.
I found a maintained aggregate and could point to evidence of it drifting or lagging.
I identified a specific modelling regret and described the shape of the decision that produced it.
I wrote the defence paragraph, and it makes a real case rather than a token one.
I can state whether the decision was wrong at the time or only wrong in hindsight, and say what distinguishes the two.

sections.title: Database Systems in Depth
sections.description: Goes under the query, into the layer where nearly every production database incident actually lives: write-ahead logging and the real cost of a commit, B-tree versus LSM engines, MVCC version bloat, connection-pool sizing by Little's Law, replication lag and read-your-own-writes routing, partition-key selection and hot partitions, and the outbox and CDC pipelines that move data out safely. Teaching examples come from a national supermarket chain; the transfer exercises move to a nationwide bike-share scheme.

learningObjectives.description: Explain how a write travels through the write-ahead log, buffer pool, and checkpoint, and predict which workloads stress which stage.
Contrast B-tree and LSM storage engines on read, write, and space amplification, select one for a stated workload, and name the operational metric that warns of its failure mode first.
Diagnose a concurrency incident — lock wait, long-running transaction, version bloat — from engine-level symptoms rather than query text.
Size and configure a connection pool from concurrency and latency figures using Little's Law, explaining why more connections can reduce throughput.
Design a read-replica routing policy that preserves read-your-own-writes under replication lag, routing by required guarantee rather than by read-versus-write.
Choose a partition key for a given dominant access pattern and identify the queries it makes expensive, plus its hot-key risk.
Design a CDC- or outbox-driven pipeline to a search index or read model, and justify it over dual writes including the at-least-once obligation it creates.
Separate an analytical workload from the transactional store and state the freshness the business is accepting, as a number in plain language.

motivationHooks.prompt:
## Why this matters

In `s3-data-layer` you learned what to model. This section is about what the engine does with it — and it exists as a separate hundred minutes because **almost every production database incident is invisible from the query layer.**

Consider what you will actually be paged for. Writes have stalled but CPU is at 12%. A query that ran in 8ms yesterday takes 4 seconds today with an unchanged plan. The connection pool is exhausted while the database reports it is mostly idle. A read replica is returning data from four minutes ago and a customer is on the phone about it.

None of those are diagnosable by looking at SQL. All of them are diagnosable one layer down.

There is a second reason this matters for your career specifically. Interview loops at large companies probe replication, partitioning, and consistency far more than they probe query syntax — because those are the decisions that don't get undone. A shard key chosen in month three constrains every query for the product's remaining life.

**Commit to an answer before you begin.**

A service runs 20 instances, each with a connection pool of 50 — a thousand possible connections — against a database with 16 CPU cores. Under load, p99 latency is 900ms.

A colleague proposes **raising** the pool to 100 per instance to handle spikes.

**What happens to throughput and p99?** Write down a direction: up, down, or unchanged.

Then answer the harder one: what pool size would you propose instead? Most engineers name a number above 50. The measured answer in the system this section is built around is **2**, and p99 falls from 900ms to 60ms.

One analyst runs one read-only query at 09:00.

By 10:50 a national supermarket chain cannot process checkouts.

The analyst's query blocked nobody. It took no locks. It was read-only. CPU never rose above 30% and no query plan changed.

The mechanism that connects those two facts is the single most useful thing in this section, and it is invisible from the query layer.

## Back to the pool

**Throughput falls and p99 rises.** The right answer was to go *down* — to about 2 per instance, 40 across the fleet.

Here is the arithmetic. Measured: 3,000 queries per second, 4ms average time *inside* the database. Little's Law gives concurrency = throughput × latency = 3,000 × 0.004 = **12 connections required**. The fleet was configured for a thousand.

That database can genuinely execute about 16 queries at once. The other 984 connections were context-switching, competing for shared memory structures, and each consuming working memory — so **coordination overhead grew while useful work did not.**

The reframing that makes it stick: **a queue has to form somewhere, and your job is to choose where.** With a small pool, requests queue in the application, where waiting is cheap, orderly, and observable. With a large pool, they queue *inside* the database, where waiting contends for shared resources and degrades every other query — including ones from services you weren't thinking about.

A connection pool is not a capacity limit. It is an **admission control mechanism**: you are deciding how much concurrency the database is permitted to attempt, and attempting less frequently completes more.

sectionSummary.content:
## What you should now believe

**A database's job is to convert your random-access mental model into sequential physical work.** The durable write is a sequential log append; the data page write is deferred and amortised. When writes are slow, look at fsync latency, checkpoint pressure, index maintenance, and compaction — not at the disk.

**MVCC did not make concurrency free; it relocated the cost.** Lock waits are visible, immediate, obvious. Version accumulation is invisible, delayed, and catastrophic — and a single open transaction is enough to cause it.

**A connection pool is admission control, not capacity.** Size it from Little's Law using in-database latency. When throughput falls as you add connections, remove connections. The queue forms somewhere; choose where.

**Consistency is a per-operation property, not a per-table one.** The same stock number routes to a replica when displayed and to the primary when it is being decremented. Route by what depends on the answer.

**Replication is not backup.** It reproduces your `DELETE` with the missing `WHERE` clause on every replica within milliseconds.

**Cardinality is not sufficient for a partition key.** It must match the dominant query's filter *and* distribute traffic evenly — and it retroactively constrains every query in the system, which is why it belongs in a design review rather than a ticket.

**Dual writes fail silently and permanently.** That property, not the failure rate, is what makes them unacceptable. The outbox converts an unsolvable cross-system atomicity problem into one the database already solves, and charges you at-least-once delivery for it.
keyTakeaways: The commit becomes durable at the fsync on the write-ahead log — that is the real cost, not the data-page write.
The six standing metrics: replication lag, oldest transaction age, buffer-pool hit ratio, lock wait time, checkpoint frequency, compaction backlog. CPU catches none of them.
Little's Law: concurrency = throughput × in-database latency. Compute the fleet total, not the per-instance number.
Route reads by required guarantee. Lag-aware replica exclusion is needed independently of read-your-own-writes.
A high-cardinality key can still be a hot partition: bananas.
An outbox gives you atomicity and hands you at-least-once delivery in exchange — the consumer must be idempotent.
If you cannot say how to rebuild a derived store and how long it would take, it is not a cache — it is an unrecoverable divergence waiting to happen.

furtherReading.title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications, Chapter 3: Storage and Retrieval
furtherReading.citation: Kleppmann, Martin. "Designing Data-Intensive Applications," Chapter 3. O'Reilly, 2017.
furtherReading.author: Martin Kleppmann
furtherReading.rationaleNote: The clearest available treatment of B-tree versus LSM internals, including the amplification tradeoffs this section tabulates. Read it if the engine comparison felt like a table to memorise rather than a mechanism you understand — Chapter 5 then covers replication in the same style.

learningExperiences.title: What Actually Happens When You Commit

contentBlocks.content:
## What you'll be able to do after this

1. **Explain how a write travels** through the write-ahead log, buffer pool, and checkpoint, and predict which workloads stress which stage.
2. **Contrast B-tree and LSM storage engines** on read, write, and space amplification, and select one for a stated workload.

Maps to `database-internals` and `data-modeling-persistence`.

## Start concrete: a cashier scans a can of beans

A supermarket till records a sale. What does the database actually do?

The naive mental model is: find the row, change it, write it to disk. If that were true, a busy Saturday — 1,800 stores, 20 tills each, several items per second — would need millions of **random** disk writes per second, scattered across the device. It would be hopeless.

What actually happens:

1. **The change is appended to the write-ahead log.** A small, sequential write to the end of a file. Sequential writes are dramatically faster than random ones, on spinning disks and SSDs alike.
2. **`fsync` is called on the log.** This is the moment the transaction becomes durable and the commit can return. **This is the real cost of a commit** — not the data write.
3. **The data page is modified in the buffer pool, in memory.** Fast. It is now "dirty": memory disagrees with disk.
4. **Later, at a checkpoint, dirty pages are written to their real locations.** In bulk, in the background, often coalescing many changes to the same page into one write.

The data page write is **deferred and amortised**, and the durability point is a sequential log append. Lose power between steps 2 and 4 and recovery replays the log. Nothing committed is lost.

**A database's job is to convert your random-access mental model into sequential physical work.** Understanding where it fails to do so is most of performance engineering.

terms.definition: The fixed-size unit the database reads and writes. You never read a row from disk, you read the page containing it.
The database's in-memory cache of pages. Most read performance is really the question of whether the page was resident.
A sequential append-only record of every change, flushed to durable storage before the change reaches data pages. The commit's real cost.
Periodically flushing modified pages to their real locations so the write-ahead log can be trimmed.
A balanced tree that updates data in place. Strong on range scans and predictable reads; high write amplification per small write.
Log-Structured Merge tree: buffers writes in memory, flushes sorted immutable files, and merges them in the background. Strong on sustained write volume.
The LSM background process that merges sorted files and discards superseded entries. Falling behind produces write stalls.
Bytes actually written to storage per byte of logical data written.

rows: high per small write — a 200-byte row rewrites an 8KB page plus every affected index page
lower at write time, but compaction rewrites data repeatedly
may check memtable plus several files, mitigated by bloom filters
excellent — data is contiguous and sorted
good, but must merge across files
can spike during compaction; deleted data lingers until merged
compaction can't keep up → read amplification climbs → write stall
very high sustained write volume, time-series, append-heavy
contentBlocks.caption: The choice follows the write-to-read ratio and the mutability of the data — not the vendor's marketing.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Believing writes are slow because disks are slow.** The durable write is a sequential log append, which is fast. The cost surfaces later and elsewhere: `fsync` latency, checkpoint storms, index maintenance across every index on the table, and LSM compaction. Blaming the disk sends you to the wrong four remedies.

**2. Forgetting that every index multiplies write cost.** You measured this in `s3-data-layer`. Here is the mechanism: each index is a separate structure that must be located, possibly split, and written on every insert.

**3. Monitoring CPU as the health signal for a database.** Nearly every incident in this section is invisible on a CPU graph. Watch replication lag, oldest transaction age, buffer-pool hit ratio, lock wait time, checkpoint frequency, and — on LSM — compaction backlog.

**4. Treating "which engine" as a separate decision from "which database."** You are usually choosing a product and the engine comes with it. What this analysis buys you is the ability to **predict how that product will fail under your workload**.

**5. Choosing an engine by benchmark.** Benchmarks measure one workload on one configuration. The differences from yours are the entire point.

interactionSequence.prompt:
A supermarket chain runs 36,000 tills. At Saturday peak they generate roughly **90,000 row updates per second** to a single database cluster.

**Predict where the bottleneck is.** Is it the physical disk writes for the changed rows, or something else? Commit to an answer and one sentence of reasoning before reading on.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
If you said "the disk writes for the changed rows," you have the naive model — and it is the model almost everyone starts with. The changed rows are **not** written to their real locations at commit time at all. They are modified in memory and flushed later, in bulk, at a checkpoint.

What is actually on the critical path is the `fsync` on the write-ahead log: a small sequential append. Everything else is deferred. So the realistic bottleneck candidates are log flush latency, checkpoint pressure when too many dirty pages accumulate, and index maintenance — because every index on the table is another structure to update per write.

Notice that three of those four are invisible if you are watching disk throughput or CPU.
hints: At the moment a commit returns, what has actually been written to durable storage?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A team's writes have become slow. CPU is at 20%, disk throughput is well below capacity, and query plans are unchanged. Which set of causes should you investigate first?
options: Disk hardware limits — the storage device has reached its IOPS ceiling.
`fsync` latency, checkpoint pressure from accumulated dirty pages, index maintenance across every index on the table, and (on LSM) compaction backlog.
Query planning overhead, since the planner runs on every statement.
Network latency between the application and the database.

optionFeedback.feedback: Disk throughput is stated as below capacity, and in any case the durable write is a sequential append — the cheapest thing a disk does. This is the "writes are slow because disks are slow" reflex.
Correct. These are the four places write cost actually surfaces, and none of them shows up on a CPU or throughput graph — which is exactly why the query layer offers no hypothesis here.
Planning overhead is real but small and would affect reads equally. It also would not correlate with a change in write performance specifically.
Network latency would raise end-to-end latency uniformly rather than degrading writes specifically, and it is upstream of anything the storage engine does.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The move to internalise: **when the query layer offers no hypothesis, go one layer down rather than staring harder at SQL.** That instinct is what this whole section is training, and the standing metric set in the common-errors box is how you make it cheap.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A team must store 90,000 telemetry events per second: append-only, never updated, queried by time range for 30 days then archived. Which engine, and what is the leading operational risk to monitor?
options: B-tree, because predictable single-key read latency matters in any production system; monitor buffer-pool hit ratio.
LSM, because sustained write volume dominates and the data is immutable; monitor compaction backlog as the leading indicator.
B-tree, because LSM write amplification is worse once background compaction is counted; monitor checkpoint frequency.
Either — at this volume the choice is dominated by team familiarity; monitor CPU.

optionFeedback.feedback: Predictable read latency is a genuine B-tree strength but not the binding constraint. Sustained write volume is, and that is precisely where in-place page modification costs most.

Correct. The write path is always sequential, the data is never mutated, and time-range queries map onto sorted files. Compaction falling behind at peak is the failure that precedes visible symptoms — and it is invisible on CPU.
Compaction does rewrite data repeatedly, but a B-tree must write a full page plus every affected index page per small write. At 90,000 events per second that is the larger cost.
Familiarity is a legitimate secondary factor, but the write-to-read ratio and immutability decide this case clearly — and CPU is the wrong metric for either engine.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: You made a version of this call in `s3-exp-engine-choice` from access patterns alone. What is new here is that you can now say **why** — and, more usefully, name the specific metric whose degradation predicts the incident. Being able to name the leading indicator is what separates having chosen an engine from being able to operate it.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: **explain to a teammate why adding an index slows writes**, using what you now know about the write path. Then connect it to the number you measured in `s3-data-layer` Part C — you timed inserts with zero, one, and four indexes. Does the mechanism explain the shape of what you measured?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The mechanism: each index is a separate B-tree. An insert must locate the correct leaf in **every** index, potentially split pages, and write those changes — and all of it goes through the write-ahead log first, so index maintenance shows up as additional log volume as well as additional page dirtying.

That is why the slowdown is roughly proportional to index count rather than a fixed overhead, and why indexes on wide or randomly-distributed columns cost more: random keys mean the target leaf is unlikely to be in the buffer pool, so the write path incurs a read first.

If your measured curve was steeper than linear, that is the likely reason. You can confirm it directly in this section's lab by measuring log bytes generated per row with and without indexes — the extra bytes are the index maintenance, made visible.
hints: How many separate structures must be located and written per insert, and what does each of those writes pass through first?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you?

workedExamples.problem: The supermarket runs two very different workloads on two systems: **(A)** a product catalogue of 400,000 items, read constantly by every till and the website, written a few thousand times a day when prices change, with range scans by category and ad-hoc filters; and **(B)** till event telemetry — every scan, void, discount, and payment step from 36,000 tills, ~90,000 events per second at peak, append-only, queried by time range for 30 days then archived. Choose an engine for each, and name what you would monitor.
steps: **Step 1 — characterise A's write-to-read ratio.** A few thousand writes per day against constant reads. Write amplification is therefore **irrelevant**: even a costly write path is invisible at that volume.

**Step 2 — characterise A's read shape.** Constant point lookups plus range scans by category plus unpredictable ad-hoc filters. A till cannot pause, so predictable single-key latency matters. → **B-tree.** The cost it is bad at simply does not exist for this workload, and it is strong at everything the workload needs.
**Step 3 — characterise B's write-to-read ratio.** 90,000 writes per second sustained, dominating everything else. This is the binding constraint and it is on the write path.

**Step 4 — characterise B's mutability and read shape.** The data is immutable — no updates, ever — and queries are time-range scans, which map directly onto sorted immutable files. → **LSM.** Writes are always sequential and never modify anything in place.

**Step 5 — name the failure mode you have just accepted, for each.** For A: checkpoint storms if dirty pages accumulate faster than they flush, and index contention. For B: **compaction falling behind at peak**, which raises read amplification and eventually stalls writes entirely.

**Step 6 — turn each failure mode into a monitored metric.** For A: checkpoint frequency and buffer-pool hit ratio. For B: **compaction backlog**, monitored as a first-class metric rather than CPU — because a node whose compaction is falling behind can sit at modest CPU right up until it stalls.
workedExamples.conclusion: **The engine choice follows the write-to-read ratio and the mutability of the data.** Steps 5 and 6 are what make this operational rather than academic: every engine choice is simultaneously a choice of failure mode, and the useful output of the analysis is the metric whose degradation warns you first. Note also that "which engine" is often not separable from "which database" — you are usually choosing a product. What this reasoning buys you is not the freedom to pick a storage engine, but the ability to **predict how the product you picked will fail under your workload.**

retrievalPractice.prompt: Trace a committed write from `COMMIT` to durable storage. At which step does the commit actually become durable, and why is that step — rather than the data-page write — the real cost?
Contrast B-tree and LSM on write amplification and failure mode under sustained load. For each, name the metric whose degradation warns you first.

learningExperiences.title: The Incident You Will Actually Get Paged For

contentBlocks.content:
## What you'll be able to do after this

**Diagnose a concurrency incident from engine-level symptoms rather than query text** — the class of incident where CPU is fine, plans are unchanged, and nothing in your SQL explains anything.

Maps to `database-internals` and back to `server-runtime-model`.

## What MVCC gives you, and what it costs

Multi-Version Concurrency Control is why readers don't block writers. When a row is updated, the old version is not overwritten — a new version is written and the old one is retained until no transaction could still need it. Readers see a consistent snapshot from when their transaction began.

This is genuinely wonderful. It also has one consequence that causes a startling number of production incidents, and the consequence is **invisible until it is severe**.

The rule that produces it: **vacuum can only reclaim a dead row version if no open transaction could still need to see it.**

So a single transaction, open since 09:00, forces the retention of every version that was live at 09:00 — for as long as it stays open. On a table taking thousands of updates per second, that is thousands of dead versions accumulating per second, for hours.

terms.definition: Multi-Version Concurrency Control: keeping multiple row versions so readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking. The cost moves into version accumulation.
Accumulated dead row versions that cannot be reclaimed, usually because a transaction has been open too long. Degrades reads system-wide.

contentBlocks.content:
## Two neighbouring diagnoses worth recognising by symptom

**Lock waits.** Queries blocked, low CPU, and a lock-monitoring view showing a chain of waiters behind one holder. Usually a transaction holding a row lock across a slow operation — very often an external HTTP call inside a transaction, which is exactly the error you met in `s3-exp-transactions`.

**Idle-in-transaction connections.** An application opens a transaction, does application work, and forgets to commit. It holds locks and blocks vacuum **while doing nothing at all**. Nearly always an application bug in error handling, where an exception path skips the commit or rollback.

Both share the shape of the main incident: the damage is done by *duration*, not by *work*.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Concluding that because MVCC removes lock waits, long transactions are harmless.** The cost moved; it did not disappear. Lock waits are visible, immediate, and obvious. Version accumulation is invisible, delayed, and catastrophic.

**2. Diagnosing an engine-level incident from query text.** Plans are unchanged in nearly all of these. If your only tool is SQL, you have no hypothesis at all.

**3. Leaving a transaction open while doing application work.** Open late, commit early — and set an idle-in-transaction timeout so the database defends itself against your application's error paths.

**4. Having no `statement_timeout`.** One unbounded analytical query can hold back vacuum for hours. A timeout converts an outage into a failed query.

**5. Alerting on CPU as the database health signal.** Every incident in this experience presents with normal CPU.

**6. Fixing the incident without adding the metric.** If oldest-transaction-age is not on a dashboard afterwards, the same incident recurs with a different query.

interactionSequence.prompt:
Read these symptoms and commit to a diagnosis before continuing.

- **09:00** — a stock analyst starts a long-running analytical query against the transactional database.
- **09:40** — database disk usage begins climbing steadily. No unusual write volume.
- **10:15** — till checkout latency rises from 20ms to 300ms. **CPU is at 30%. No query plans have changed.**
- **10:50** — checkouts begin timing out. Disk usage has grown 400GB.

**What is happening, and what is the single thing you would check first?**

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Start with what is **not** wrong, because it eliminates most hypotheses immediately: CPU is fine, plans are unchanged, write volume is normal. So this is not a query problem — which is precisely why spending the first hour reading SQL wastes it.

Growing disk with normal CPU and unchanged plans is the signature of **version bloat**. The single thing to check is the **age of the oldest open transaction**, which every mature database can report. There is one, open since 09:00, and it belongs to the analyst.

If you diagnosed it correctly, notice what made it possible: not knowing more SQL, but having a model one layer below the query. If you didn't, that is the point of the experience.
hints: Which of the four symptoms rules out the most hypotheses?
What can prevent a database from reclaiming space it should be able to reclaim?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Disk usage on your primary has grown 300GB in two hours, point-lookup latency has tripled, CPU is at 25%, and no query plans have changed. What do you check first?
options: Whether a missing index is causing full table scans.
Whether the connection pool is exhausted.
The age of the oldest open transaction, because a long-running transaction prevents reclamation of dead row versions.
Nothing urgent — MVCC means readers do not block writers, so a long query is harmless.

optionFeedback.feedback: Plans are unchanged, so indexes are not the difference between yesterday and today. A missing index also would not grow disk usage.
Pool exhaustion produces queuing and timeouts, not disk growth. Worth checking later, but it cannot explain 300GB.
Correct. Growing disk with normal CPU and unchanged plans is the signature of version bloat: every dead version since the old transaction began must be retained, and reads then traverse them.
MVCC removed the lock waits but relocated the cost into version accumulation, which is invisible until it is severe. This is exactly how one analyst's query degrades a transactional system.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Note the shape of the correct reasoning: you got there by **elimination on the symptoms that were normal**, not by pattern-matching the symptom that was abnormal. Normal CPU plus unchanged plans is a strong signal in its own right — it rules out the entire query layer in one step.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: You resolve the bloat incident by terminating the analyst's transaction. Latency recovers. What must you do so that the same incident does not recur with a different query?
options: Ask analysts to notify the on-call engineer before running long queries.
Set a statement timeout and an idle-in-transaction timeout, give analysts a replica or warehouse, and alert on oldest-transaction-age as a standing metric.
Increase the frequency of the vacuum process so it reclaims space faster.
Add more disk capacity so that future bloat does not exhaust storage.

optionFeedback.feedback: A process control that depends on people remembering, in an organisation where the analyst may not know the query is long. It will hold until the first busy week.

Correct, and it addresses all three layers: the database defends itself with timeouts, the workload is moved somewhere it cannot cause this, and the metric makes the next occurrence visible in minutes rather than hours.
Vacuum frequency is not the constraint — vacuum was running and was **unable** to reclaim anything, because an open transaction still required those versions. Running it more often does nothing.
Disk was a symptom, not the cause. More disk buys a longer runway to the same outage, and does nothing about the latency degradation, which is what actually hurt.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Option C is the instructive wrong answer: it is a **correct-sounding remedy that addresses a mechanism that was never the problem.** Vacuum was working perfectly and reclaiming nothing, which is only comprehensible one layer below the query. That gap between plausible and correct is why this competency is assessed at the `analyze` level.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

workedExamples.problem: Work the full incident: from the four symptoms above to a resolution and a permanent fix. Show the causal chain explicitly — the goal is a diagnosis you could defend in a post-mortem, not a lucky guess.
steps: **Step 1 — note what is not wrong.** CPU is at 30%. Query plans are unchanged. Write volume is normal. This eliminates the entire query layer, which is why looking at SQL would waste the first hour.
**Step 2 — find the oldest transaction.** Every mature database can report currently-open transactions and their age. There is one, open since 09:00, belonging to the analyst.

**Step 3 — reason about why that matters.** Vacuum can only reclaim a dead row version if no open transaction could still need it. The analyst's transaction began at 09:00, so **every version live at 09:00 must be retained** for the entire duration of their query. On a table taking thousands of updates per second, dead versions accumulate at thousands per second, for two hours.

**Step 4 — connect bloat to latency.** Queries scanning that table now traverse a huge number of dead versions to find live rows. Each read touches far more pages, the buffer pool's hit rate collapses, and reads that were served from memory now go to disk. That is the 20ms → 300ms.
**Step 5 — resolve.** Terminate the long-running transaction. Vacuum reclaims. Latency recovers within minutes; disk space recovers more slowly.

**Step 6 — fix it permanently, at three layers.** Set a `statement_timeout` and an idle-in-transaction timeout so no session can do this again. Give analysts a dedicated replica or warehouse so the workload never touches the primary. Alert on **oldest-transaction-age** as a standing metric.
workedExamples.conclusion: **MVCC did not make concurrency free; it relocated the cost from lock waits to version accumulation.** The analyst blocked nobody — that part worked exactly as designed. But the cost moved from something visible, immediate, and obvious to something invisible, delayed, and catastrophic. Step 6 is what makes this a fix rather than a recovery: without the timeout the incident recurs, and without the metric it recurs *undetected for the same two hours*. Note also the connection back to `s3-exp-transactions`: long-running transactions were dangerous there because they hold locks. This is the second, subtler reason, and it does not require holding a single lock.

retrievalPractice.prompt: A single idle-but-open transaction is degrading an entire database. Explain the four-step causal chain from 'transaction stays open' to 'unrelated point lookups got slower'.
Name the six standing metrics that predict database incidents. Which one would have caught the bloat incident, and why does CPU catch none of them?

learningExperiences.title: Why More Connections Make Things Slower

contentBlocks.content:
## What you'll be able to do after this

**Size a connection pool from concurrency and latency figures**, and explain why more connections can reduce throughput.

Maps to `database-internals` and `scalability-capacity-tradeoffs`. This is **hop ⑤** from `s1-server-mental-model`, finally computed rather than acknowledged.

## Little's Law

Every database connection costs memory, scheduler attention, and — in some engines — an OS process. They are not free, and they are **not the same thing as concurrent requests**.

For a system in steady state:

> **concurrency = throughput × latency**

If you need 3,000 queries per second and each takes 4ms *inside the database*, the concurrency you require is:

`3,000 × 0.004 = 12 connections`

Not 200. Twelve.

The word doing the work is **inside**. Most of a request's life is not spent in the database, so request concurrency and database concurrency are different numbers — often by an order of magnitude.

terms.definition: Concurrency equals throughput times latency. The arithmetic that sizes a connection pool from measured in-database time.
A fixed, reusable set of database connections shared by all requests on an instance. Size it with Little's Law, not with request concurrency.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Sizing the pool by request concurrency.** "We handle 50 concurrent requests, so we need 50 connections" conflates two different numbers. Use in-database latency.

**2. Assuming idle connections are free.** They consume memory and, in some engines, a process each — and under the spike they will not be idle, which is precisely the saturation scenario.

**3. Multiplying without noticing.** Twenty instances with a pool of 50 is **1,000 connections** against one database. Always compute the fleet total, not the per-instance number.

**4. Adding database CPU to service a pool size the arithmetic says you don't need.** Buying hardware to fix a config value.

**5. Concluding the queue can be eliminated.** It cannot. A queue forms somewhere whenever demand exceeds capacity — **your job is to choose where.** In the application it is cheap, orderly, and visible. In the database it is expensive and degrades everyone.

**6. Ignoring that transactions hold connections for their whole life.** A slow external call inside a transaction occupies a pool slot for its full duration. That is the `s3-data-layer` boundary rule, arriving from the pool's side.

interactionSequence.prompt:
A service runs **20 instances**, each with a connection pool of **50**, against a database with **16 CPU cores**. Under load, p99 latency is 900ms.

A colleague proposes raising the pool to 100 per instance to handle spikes.

**Predict what happens to throughput and p99.** Commit to a direction — up, down, or unchanged — and one sentence of reasoning.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
First, do the multiplication most people skip: 20 × 50 is already **1,000 connections** against a 16-core machine. Doubling makes it 2,000.

That database can genuinely execute about 16 queries at once. The other 984 are context-switching, competing for shared memory structures, and each consuming its own working memory. **Throughput falls as connections rise past saturation**, because coordination overhead grows while useful work does not.

So the prediction is: throughput down, p99 up. And the counterintuitive corollary — which the worked example demonstrates — is that reducing the pool to **2 per instance** takes p99 from 900ms to around 60ms. If that direction surprised you, the worked example is the important part of this experience.
hints: How many queries can a 16-core database genuinely execute at the same instant?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Your service does 2,000 queries per second with an average in-database time of 5ms. A colleague proposes raising the pool from 10 to 200 per instance across 20 instances. What is the right response?
options: Little's Law says you need about 10 connections total; 4,000 would put the database far past saturation and reduce throughput.
Agree — a larger pool can only help, since extra connections sit idle when unused.
Agree, but add database CPU cores in proportion.
Disagree, and move to a document store, which handles high connection counts better.

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. 2,000 × 0.005 = 10. Past the point where the database can execute queries in parallel, extra connections add context-switching and shared-structure contention while adding no useful work. Queue in the application, where waiting is cheap and visible.
Idle connections still consume memory and, in some engines, a process each — and under the spike they will not be idle, which is exactly the saturation scenario.
This treats the symptom as a capacity shortage when the concurrency arithmetic says otherwise, buying hardware to service a pool size you do not need.
This is a configuration error, not an engine limitation. Migrating databases to avoid computing a pool size imports an enormous migration for a two-line change.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The sentence to carry: **a queue has to form somewhere; your job is to choose where.** In the application it is cheap, orderly, and observable — you can see the depth and alert on it. Inside the database it contends for shared structures and degrades every other query, including ones from services you weren't thinking about.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Your Little's Law calculation says you need 30 connections across the fleet, but you have 200 application instances and each needs at least one connection. What is the right resolution?
options: Accept 200 connections; one per instance is the irreducible minimum.
Reduce the instance count until the numbers reconcile.
Put an external connection pooler in front of the database, multiplexing many application connections onto few database connections.
Raise the database's max connections limit and accept the overhead as the cost of horizontal scaling.

optionFeedback.feedback: It is the irreducible minimum *for direct connections* — which is exactly the constraint an external pooler removes.
This subordinates a real capacity decision to a config value, and instance count is usually driven by request handling rather than database concurrency.
Correct. This is precisely the problem external poolers exist for: application instances connect to the pooler, and the pooler maintains a small set of real database connections shared across them.
Raising the limit permits the connections; it does not make the database able to use them. You would be authorising the saturation the arithmetic warned you about.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Worth noticing: the tension here is real and common — horizontal scaling of stateless instances (`s1-server-mental-model`) pushes connection count up, while database concurrency arithmetic pushes it down. An external pooler is the standard resolution, and recognising that two correct pieces of reasoning can pull in opposite directions is itself part of the competency.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: **explain the apparent paradox** — how can *reducing* the connection pool improve both throughput and latency? Explain it to someone who has just watched you shrink a pool during an incident and thinks you have made things worse.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The core of a good explanation: **the work does not disappear, and the queue does not disappear — the queue moves.**

With a large pool, requests queue *inside* the database, where hundreds of sessions contend for shared memory structures, thrash the scheduler, and each consume working memory. Every query gets slower, including the ones that were already running.

With a small pool, requests queue *in the application*, waiting to acquire a connection. That wait is cheap — it consumes no database resources at all — and the queries that do get through run at full speed against an unsaturated database. Total throughput rises because the database is doing useful work rather than coordination.

The reframing that makes it click for most people: a connection pool is not a capacity limit, it is an **admission control mechanism**. You are deciding how much concurrency the database is allowed to attempt, and attempting less can complete more.
hints: If the requests are not being served, where are they waiting instead — and what is that waiting costing?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you?

workedExamples.problem: The supermarket's pricing service runs **20 instances, each with a pool of 50** — 1,000 possible connections against a database with **16 CPU cores**. Under load, p99 latency is **900ms**. Fix it, and explain why the fix works.
steps: **Step 1 — find the reasoning that produced the 50.** "We handle 50 concurrent requests per instance, so we need 50 connections." This conflates request concurrency with database concurrency: most of a request's life is not spent in the database.

**Step 2 — compute what 1,000 connections do to a 16-core machine.** The database can genuinely execute about 16 queries at once. The other 984 are context-switching, competing for shared memory structures, and each consuming its own working memory. Throughput **falls** as connections rise past saturation, because coordination overhead grows while useful work does not.

**Step 3 — apply Little's Law with measured figures.** Measured: 3,000 queries per second, 4ms average in-database time. Required concurrency = 3,000 × 0.004 = **12**. Add headroom for variance: perhaps 25–30 total across the fleet.
**Step 4 — reduce the pool to 2 per instance** (40 total) and re-measure. **p99 falls to 60ms. Throughput rises.**

**Step 5 — explain the apparent paradox.** With a small pool, requests queue *in the application*, where waiting is cheap, orderly, and observable. With a large pool, they queue *inside the database*, where waiting is expensive, contends for shared resources, and degrades everyone. **A queue has to form somewhere; your job is to choose where.**

**Step 6 — handle the case where the arithmetic and the fleet disagree.** If you have 200 instances and each needs at least one connection, direct connections cannot reconcile with a 30-connection target. That is what an external connection pooler is for: application instances connect to it, and it maintains a small set of real database connections shared across all of them.
workedExamples.conclusion: **Pool size should be derived from Little's Law using in-database latency, not from request concurrency.** When throughput drops as you add connections, you are past saturation and the remedy is to remove connections, not add them. The reframing worth keeping: **a connection pool is an admission control mechanism, not a capacity limit** — you are choosing how much concurrency the database is permitted to attempt, and attempting less frequently completes more.

fadedVariant.problem: A different service: the supermarket's loyalty API. **12 instances**, pool of **25** each. Measured: **800 queries per second**, average in-database time **9ms**. The database has **8 cores**. p99 is 340ms and the team wants to raise the pool. Work out the right answer.
givenSteps: **Step 1 — the reasoning behind the 25** was request concurrency per instance, not measured in-database time.
**Step 5 — the principle** is that a queue forms somewhere and you are choosing where it forms.
blankedStepPrompts: **Step 2 —** compute the current fleet-wide connection total and compare it to what the database can genuinely execute in parallel.
**Step 3 —** apply Little's Law to get the required concurrency, then state a pool size per instance including headroom.
**Step 6 —** the team says a pool of 2 per instance 'feels dangerously small' and asks what happens during a traffic spike. Answer them.
blankedStepAnswers: 12 instances × 25 = **300 possible connections** against an 8-core database, which can genuinely execute roughly 8 queries at once. Around 292 would be contending rather than working — well past saturation, which is why raising the pool would make p99 worse rather than better.

800 × 0.009 = **7.2 connections** required fleet-wide. With headroom for variance, call it 15–20 total, which is **1 to 2 per instance** across 12 instances. The current 300 is roughly twenty times the requirement.

During a spike, requests queue in the application waiting to acquire a connection — and that is the desired behaviour, not a failure. The queue is cheap (it consumes no database resources), it is observable (you can measure acquisition wait time and alert on it), and the queries that do run complete at full speed rather than all of them slowing down together. The alternative — a large pool — means the spike is absorbed *inside* the database, where every concurrent query degrades and p99 rises for everyone including unrelated services. What the team should add alongside the smaller pool is a metric on pool acquisition wait time and a sensible acquisition timeout, so a genuine capacity problem surfaces as a fast, visible failure rather than as uniform slowness.

retrievalPractice.prompt: State Little's Law and use it to size a pool for 2,000 queries per second at 5ms in-database latency. Then explain why doubling that pool would reduce throughput.

learningExperiences.title: Read Replicas and the Guarantee You Just Lost

contentBlocks.content:
## What you'll be able to do after this

**Design a read-replica routing policy that preserves read-your-own-writes under replication lag** — and distinguish replication from backup.

Maps to `replication-partitioning` and `state-caching-consistency`.

## Replicas are not free reads

A replica applies the primary's log stream and serves reads. This genuinely adds read capacity. It also introduces a guarantee you just lost.

**A replica is behind.** Usually milliseconds. During a bulk backfill — exactly the kind you wrote in `s3-exp-migrations` — a large `DELETE`, or an index build, it can be minutes.

The user-visible failure is specific and reliably reproducible: a customer updates their loyalty address, the write goes to the primary, the page redirects, the read goes to a replica 200ms behind, and **the old address is displayed**. The customer edits again. Now you have a support ticket and possibly a duplicate record.

rows: A user reading data they just changed
contentBlocks.caption: Route by required guarantee, not by read-versus-write. Note rows 5 and 6: the SAME data, routed two different ways.

contentBlocks.content:
Those two bolded rows are the important pair. **The same data is routed differently depending on what depends on the answer.** Displaying "3 left in stock" slightly stale is a UX detail. Deducting stock at checkout on stale data oversells the item.

Recognising that **consistency is a per-operation property, not a per-table one** is the single most useful idea in this section — and it is the seed of the formal treatment in `s8-distributed-programming`.

## Three implementable techniques for read-your-own-writes

1. **Sticky-to-primary window.** After a user writes, route *that user's* reads to the primary for N seconds, where N exceeds typical lag. Simple, effective, costs some primary read load. Store the marker in the session or shared cache.
2. **Log-position tokens.** On write, capture the primary's log position and return it to the client or store it in the session. On read, wait until the chosen replica has applied at least that position, or fall back to the primary. Precise, more machinery.
3. **Route by lag.** Continuously measure each replica's lag and exclude replicas above a threshold from the pool. **Necessary regardless of the other two**, and the mechanism that saves you during a backfill.

terms.definition: The guarantee that after you write something, you see it on your next read. The guarantee most often broken by naive replica routing.
The property that copies converge after a bounded delay. Data from a moment ago, not incorrect data.
The strongest single-object guarantee: once a write completes, every subsequent read anywhere observes it.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Routing all reads to replicas because "reads scale on replicas."** Any read whose result the user just caused must be linearizable. Route by required guarantee, per operation.

**2. Adding a cache in front of a stale read to make it faster.** You have added a *second* layer of staleness. Recall from `s2` and `s3` that copies compound.

**3. Adding more replicas to reduce lag.** Lag is not caused by replica read load. More replicas do not reduce it, and during a backfill all of them lag together.

**4. Treating replication as backup.** This one ends careers — see below.

**5. Forgetting that your own backfill is the biggest lag source you will ever create.** The batched backfill from `s3-exp-migrations` must monitor replica lag between batches and pause if it climbs.

**6. Routing by table rather than by operation.** The stock-level rows above are the counterexample: one table, two required guarantees.

contentBlocks.title: Replication is not backup
contentBlocks.content:
Replication **faithfully reproduces every operation**, including `DELETE FROM customers` with a missing `WHERE` clause, and including corruption. It arrives on every replica within milliseconds.

Backups defend against a **different failure class**: human error, application bugs, corruption. They must be point-in-time, tested by actual restoration, and stored where a compromised primary cannot reach them.

An untested backup is a belief, not a backup.

interactionSequence.prompt: A customer updates their delivery address, is redirected to a confirmation page, and sees the old address. What is the correct fix?
options: Add a cache in front of the read so it is faster next time.
Increase the number of read replicas so reads are spread more thinly.
Route this user's reads to the primary for a short window after their write, or wait for the replica to reach the write's log position.
Route all reads to the primary, since replicas cannot be trusted for correctness.

optionFeedback.feedback: This makes it worse: a cache in front of a stale read adds a second layer of staleness.
Lag here is not caused by replica load, and more replicas do not reduce it. This is 'read replicas scale reads for free', with the free part being exactly what is failing.
Correct. The guarantee needed is per-operation: any read whose content the user just caused must come from a source that has definitely applied their write.
It works, but discards the read capacity replicas provide and does not scale. The skill is routing by required guarantee, not abandoning replicas.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Option D is the overcorrection worth naming: it is *correct* and it throws away the entire benefit. A lot of engineering judgement consists of resisting the fix that works by removing the capability.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: During a disaster-recovery review, a team states that their three synchronous replicas make separate backups unnecessary. What is the strongest objection?
options: Replicas can lag, so a failover might lose recent writes.
Replication reproduces destructive operations and corruption on every replica within milliseconds, so it defends against hardware loss but not against human error or application bugs.
Three replicas is insufficient; five would be needed for true durability.
Backups are only required for regulatory compliance, not for technical recovery.

optionFeedback.feedback: True and secondary. Lag is a real concern at failover, but it does not touch the class of failure that makes backups necessary.

Correct. A DELETE with a missing WHERE clause, or silent corruption, arrives everywhere at wire speed. Backups must be point-in-time, isolated from the primary's credentials, and verified by actual restore drills.
Adding replicas does not change the failure class: all of them faithfully reproduce the same mistake.
Compliance may require them, but the technical case stands on its own — an untested backup is a belief rather than a backup.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The question to ask in any DR review, which cuts through the whole discussion: **"what do your replicas contain 200 milliseconds after an accidental mass delete?"** The answer is "the accidental mass delete," and it ends the debate faster than any amount of theory.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt:
Two engineers design read routing for a supermarket's stock system.

**Engineer A:** "Route all reads to replicas and all writes to the primary. That's what replicas are for, and it's a rule anyone can follow."

**Engineer B:** "Route by what depends on the answer. The stock number on the product page goes to a replica. The stock check inside the checkout transaction goes to the primary. Same table, same column, different routing."

**Which would you ship?** Then the harder question: **A's rule has one genuine advantage over B's. What is it, and does it outweigh the cost?**

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Ship B. A's rule oversells stock: the checkout stock check reads a lagging replica, two customers both see the last unit available, and both buy it.

But A's genuine advantage is real and worth naming: **it is a rule that requires no judgement.** Every engineer on the team can apply it correctly without understanding replication, it can be enforced mechanically in a data-access layer, and it never drifts. B's approach requires every engineer to correctly classify every read forever — and the failure mode when someone classifies wrong is silent, which is the worst kind.

So the honest answer is not "B is right and A is naive." It is that B is correct and **B's correctness has an ongoing cost that must be paid with tooling rather than discipline** — a typed distinction in the data layer between a consistent read and an eventual one, so that routing is a property of the call rather than a decision someone remembers to make. If you cannot afford that tooling, A plus a small explicit list of primary-only reads is a defensible compromise, and saying so is better engineering than pretending discipline scales.
hints: What happens to B's approach when the team grows from four engineers to forty?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

workedExamples.problem: The supermarket adds two read replicas to relieve the primary. Within a week: customers report seeing stale loyalty balances after redeeming points, and during a Tuesday-night data migration the mobile app showed prices from twenty minutes earlier. Design the routing policy that fixes both.
steps: **Step 1 — classify the two failures separately.** The loyalty balance is a **read-your-own-writes** violation: the user caused the change and is reading it back. The stale prices are a **lag magnitude** problem: the backfill pushed all replicas minutes behind, so even reads that tolerate seconds of staleness became wrong.

**Step 2 — build the routing table by required guarantee.** Go operation by operation, not table by table. Anything inside a write transaction: primary. A user reading data they just changed: primary or a lag-aware replica. Another user's data, catalogue browsing, pre-checkout stock display: replica. Analytics: dedicated replica.

**Step 3 — find the pair that shares a table but not a guarantee.** Stock level *displayed* on the product page tolerates staleness; stock level *checked at checkout* does not, because deducting against a stale read oversells. Same table, same column, two routes. If your table has no such pair, look harder — most do.

**Step 4 — implement read-your-own-writes for failure one.** Simplest sufficient mechanism: after a user writes, route that user's reads to the primary for N seconds, N greater than typical lag, with the marker in their session. Log-position tokens are more precise if you need them.

**Step 5 — implement lag-aware exclusion for failure two.** Continuously measure each replica's lag and remove any replica above a threshold from the read pool. This is what saves you during the backfill — and note that neither of the read-your-own-writes techniques would have: the mobile app users were not reading their own writes.

**Step 6 — close the loop with the migration procedure.** The backfill from `s3-exp-migrations` must monitor replica lag **between batches** and pause when it climbs. Your own migrations are the largest lag source you will ever create, and they are entirely under your control.
workedExamples.conclusion: **Route by required guarantee, per operation — never by read-versus-write, and never by table.** Step 5 is the one teams omit: they implement read-your-own-writes, consider replication solved, and are then surprised by an incident where nobody was reading their own writes at all. Lag-aware exclusion is necessary independently, because lag has causes that have nothing to do with any individual user's session — chief among them your own backfills.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Give three techniques for preserving read-your-own-writes on a replica-backed system. Which one also protects you during a bulk backfill, and why do the other two not?

learningExperiences.title: Choosing the Key You Can't Change

contentBlocks.content:
## What you'll be able to do after this

**Choose a partition key for a stated dominant access pattern**, identify the queries it makes expensive, and assess its hot-key risk.

Maps to `replication-partitioning` and `data-modeling-persistence`. This is the most consequential irreversible decision in the course.

## The rule that governs everything

When one node can't hold the data or the write volume, you partition: rows are distributed across nodes by a **partition key**.

> **A query that includes the partition key goes to one node. A query that doesn't must ask every node.**

That second case — **scatter-gather** — is slow, scales badly with node count, and is limited by the slowest node. It does not get better as you add capacity; it gets worse.

terms.definition: The column whose value determines which partition a row lives on. Must match the dominant query's filter and distribute traffic evenly.
A query that must ask every partition and merge results, because it cannot be routed by partition key.
One partition receiving disproportionate traffic, saturating while the others idle.
How far behind a replica is from the primary, in time or log position. Milliseconds normally, minutes during a backfill or index build.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Choosing a key by cardinality alone.** `product_id` is high cardinality and still gives you the bananas problem. The key must match the dominant query's filter **and** distribute traffic evenly.

**2. Believing sharding can be added later without cost.** The partition key retroactively constrains **every query in your system**. Adding it means re-examining all of them and rewriting the ones that no longer route.

**3. Trying to find one key that serves every access pattern.** Usually impossible. The correct output of the analysis is often "this key, and these queries move to a separate read model."

**4. Forgetting that transactions across partitions are hard or unavailable.** A key that splits two entities you need to update atomically has created a distributed transaction problem — see `s8-distributed-programming`.

**5. Partitioning before doing the arithmetic.** You did capacity estimation in `s5-distributed-resilience`... which comes *after* this section in delivery order, so do it now: most systems are one or two orders of magnitude smaller than they feel.

**6. Ignoring rebalancing.** Adding partitions later means moving data. How much, and can it be done online? Ask before you commit.

interactionSequence.prompt:
A supermarket chain wants to partition a 40-billion-row sales line-item table. A colleague proposes `product_id`, arguing it has excellent cardinality — hundreds of thousands of distinct values, evenly spread across the catalogue.

**Predict what goes wrong.** Be specific about which real-world product breaks it.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
**Bananas.**

A handful of products account for a huge share of all line items in any supermarket — bananas, milk, bread, carrier bags. Those partitions receive orders of magnitude more traffic than the partition holding artisanal fish sauce, and **they cannot be split further** because every banana line item must live on the banana partition by definition.

So cardinality was high and the distribution was still catastrophic. The two are different properties: cardinality counts distinct values, but what matters is the distribution of *traffic across* those values.

The second failure, which is easier to miss: every store-level operational query — "all sales at store 412 last week" — becomes a scatter-gather across every partition. That is most of the operational traffic.
hints: Which products does a supermarket sell far more of than any other?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: You are partitioning an events table. A colleague proposes `user_id` because it has 40 million distinct values. What is the strongest concern?
options: `user_id` is too high cardinality, which fragments data across too many partitions.
Cardinality alone does not qualify a key: the dominant queries must filter on it, and traffic per user must be even.
It is fine — high cardinality is the requirement for a good partition key.
Partition keys can be changed later if it does not work out, so the risk is low.

optionFeedback.feedback: High cardinality does not fragment partitions; rows are grouped by hash or range into a fixed number of partitions regardless of how many distinct key values exist.
Correct, and it names both tests. Many real systems have a few enormously active accounts — a corporate integration, a bot, a reseller — whose partition saturates while the rest idle.
This is the misconception stated directly. A high-cardinality key with skewed access still produces a hot partition, and a key the dominant query does not filter on makes every read a scatter-gather.
This is the more expensive error. Changing a partition key means physically redistributing all data and re-examining every query for whether it still routes.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Two tests, both required: **does the dominant query filter on this key**, and **is traffic across key values even?** Cardinality is a precondition for the second, never a substitute for either.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Your analysis shows no single partition key serves both the store-level operational queries and the product-level analytical ones. What is the correct conclusion?
options: Choose the key that serves the more important queries and accept scatter-gather on the rest.
Partition by a hash of the transaction ID for even distribution, and serve the analytical access patterns from a separate purpose-built system fed from this one.
Do not partition at all until a single key can be found that serves everything.
Partition twice — maintain two copies of the table with different keys, kept in sync by the application.

optionFeedback.feedback: Defensible only if the rejected queries are genuinely rare. Here the analytical queries are a whole category of business need, and scatter-gather across every partition does not improve as the cluster grows.

Correct, and this is the normal situation rather than a failure of analysis. Stop trying to make one store serve two workload shapes — which is the same conclusion you reached in `s3-exp-engine-choice`, now with partitioning as the forcing constraint.
Sometimes right! If the arithmetic says a single node suffices, not partitioning is the correct answer. But it is not a resolution to the conflict — it just defers it.

Application-maintained dual copies are dual writes, which fail silently and permanently the first time the second write fails. If you need two representations, derive one from the other with a pipeline.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Option D is the trap that looks like initiative. Keeping two partitioned copies in step from application code is the dual-write problem at scale — and the next experience is entirely about why that fails and what to do instead.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

workedExamples.problem: Partition the supermarket's 40-billion-row sales line-item table. Evaluate three candidate keys against the two operational query shapes: **"all sales at store 412 last week"** and **"all sales of product 88213 chain-wide."**
steps:
**Candidate A — `store_id`.** Single-partition: "all sales at store 412 last week" ✅ — the dominant operational query. Scatter-gather: "all sales of product 88213 chain-wide" ❌.

**Hot partition risk: severe.** Store sizes vary by 50×, so the flagship store's partition takes vastly more traffic than a village shop's and one node saturates while others idle. Worse, **opening a new megastore creates a new hotspot you cannot rebalance away**, because all its data must live together by definition.

**Candidate B — `product_id`.** Single-partition: "all sales of product 88213 chain-wide" ✅. Scatter-gather: every store-level query ❌ — which is most of the operational traffic.

**Hot partition risk: severe and predictable.** Bananas. A handful of products account for a huge share of all line items, and they cannot be split further.

**Candidate C — `hash(transaction_id)`.** Even distribution ✅ — transaction IDs are uniformly distributed by construction, so no hot partitions. Single-partition: retrieving one transaction ✅. Scatter-gather: **both** the store query and the product query ❌.
**Step 4 — accept that no key serves both.** This is the normal situation, not a failure of analysis. Continuing to search for a perfect key is the most common way this decision goes wrong.

**Step 5 — resolve by splitting the workloads.** Partition the transactional store by `hash(transaction_id)` for even write distribution and fast single-transaction lookup — that is the OLTP need, and it is what the transactional store exists for. Serve the store-level and product-level analytical queries from a **separate, purpose-built system fed from this one**.

**Step 6 — name what you have just committed to.** A synchronization pipeline, with its own freshness guarantee, rebuild path, and monitoring. That obligation is real and is built in the next experience.
workedExamples.conclusion: **Cardinality is not sufficient**: `product_id` had high cardinality and produced a catastrophic hot partition, because what matters is the distribution of traffic *across* key values, not the count of them. The key must match the dominant query's filter **and** distribute evenly. And note why this belongs in a design review rather than an implementation ticket: **the partition key retroactively constrains every query in your system.** Adding partitioning to an existing system means re-examining every query you have and rewriting the ones that no longer route — which is why "we can shard later" is the most expensive sentence in this section.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Why is high cardinality insufficient for a partition key? Give a concrete example of a high-cardinality key that produces a hot partition, and name the two tests a candidate key must pass.

transferExercises.context: A nationwide bike-share scheme — deliberately outside the supermarket domain used in the teaching examples.
transferExercises.scenario:
A bike-share operates in **40 cities** with **90,000 bikes** and **6,000 docking stations**. Every bike emits a GPS and status ping every 10 seconds while in motion; each completed ride produces a ride record. Peak: roughly **300,000 pings per second** across the network.

The system must support:

- **(a)** "Where is bike 44192 right now?" — operations, constant, must be instant.
- **(b)** "Which bikes are currently at station Kreuzberg-14?" — the rider app, very high volume.
- **(c)** "All rides taken by user 8813 in the last year" — account history.
- **(d)** "Average ride duration by city by month" — the analytics team.
- **(e)** "Which docks have been empty for more than 45 minutes?" — the rebalancing van dispatcher, every 5 minutes.
transferExercises.task:
1. For the ping stream, choose B-tree or LSM. Justify from the write-to-read ratio and the mutability of the data, and name the specific operational metric you would monitor as the leading indicator of trouble.
2. Propose a partition key for the ping data. List which of (a)–(e) become single-partition and which become scatter-gather. Then identify the hot-partition risk and say whether it is tolerable.
3. There is no single key that serves all five. Name which queries you are **deliberately not** going to serve from this store, and describe where they should be served from instead.
4. Query (e) is the one most likely to be designed badly. Explain why it resists partitioning, and propose a design that makes it cheap.
5. Rides are billed. Explain why the billing read at ride-end must not go to a replica, using the routing table from this section, and contrast it with the map view in the rider app.
6. Explain why keying the ping stream by `city_id` would be a poor choice, even though it makes query (d) single-partition.
successCriteria: LSM chosen for the ping stream, justified by sustained write volume and immutability; compaction backlog named as the leading indicator rather than CPU.
A defensible partition key proposed — commonly `bike_id` or a hash of it — with an explicit list of which queries route and which scatter.
Hot-partition risk assessed with reference to traffic distribution across key values, not merely cardinality.
States that queries (d) and (e), and probably (b), will not be served from the transactional ping store, and names a derived read model or analytical store as their home.

Explains that (e) is an absence query — it asks about docks where nothing has happened — which cannot be routed by any key on the event stream, and proposes maintaining current dock state as a separate small, frequently-updated dataset.

Billing read correctly assigned to the primary inside the transaction on linearizability grounds; map view assigned to a replica on eventual-consistency grounds, with the contrast explicitly drawn as the same data routed two ways.

Explains that `city_id` has catastrophically low cardinality (40 values) and highly skewed traffic, so a handful of large cities would saturate their partitions while small ones idle, and no further splitting is possible.

learningExperiences.title: Getting Data Out Safely — and Keeping Analytics Off Your Primary

contentBlocks.content:
## What you'll be able to do after this

1. **Design a CDC- or outbox-driven pipeline** to a search index or read model, and justify it over dual writes.
2. **Separate an analytical workload** from the transactional store and state the freshness the business is accepting.

Maps to `transactional-analytical-separation`, `event-driven-processing`, and `architecture-decision-communication`.

You derived the outbox from first principles in `s3-exp-transactions` — from two ordinary rules: don't put side effects in transactions, and don't lose work. Here you build it.
## The wrong way, which nearly everyone tries first

contentBlocks.caption: Dual writes — fails silently and permanently
contentBlocks.content:
await db.updateProduct(product);        // ✅ succeeds
await searchIndex.update(product);      // ❌ times out

The database has the new price. The search index has the old one.

There is **no transaction spanning both systems**, so there is nothing to roll back, no error surfaced to the user (their write succeeded!), and no record that divergence occurred. The customer sees £2.40 in search and pays £2.65 at the till.

**The defining property is that it fails silently and permanently.** Not that it fails — everything fails sometimes — but that nothing tells you, and nothing reconciles it.

contentBlocks.caption: Fix 1 — the transactional outbox

contentBlocks.content:
Now the change and the intent-to-publish are **atomic**: either both happened or neither did.

A separate publisher process polls the outbox, pushes to the search index or a message broker, and marks rows as sent. If the publisher crashes mid-flight, it retries — which means **at-least-once delivery**, and therefore **the consumer must be idempotent**. That obligation is not optional, and it is developed fully in `s8-distributed-programming`.

**Fix 2 — Change Data Capture.** Read the database's own replication log and turn committed changes into a stream. Nothing to add to application code; captures changes made by *any* writer including manual fixes; no polling load. The costs are real operational machinery, schema-change handling in the pipeline, and a stream shaped like your **tables** rather than your domain — which reintroduces a version of the storage-leakage problem from `s2-api-contracts` at the data layer, since downstream consumers now depend on your column names.

**Choosing:** outbox when you want domain-shaped events and control over the payload, and when you're already writing the code. CDC when you need to capture *all* changes regardless of origin, when you can't modify the writing application, or when you need the throughput.
## Why analytics on the primary is worse than it looks

terms.definition: Writing an event-to-publish row inside the same transaction as the business change, then publishing it separately. Yields at-least-once delivery.
Reading the database's replication log to produce a stream of change events, capturing changes made by any writer.
Every message delivered one or more times. What you actually get, which is why consumers must be idempotent.
A copy of data kept closer to the reader than the source of truth. Definitionally stale by some amount, and discardable because it can be repopulated on demand.

rows: billions of rows, few columns, aggregated
**small hot working set, high hit rate**
contentBlocks.caption: The last row is the operational crux.

contentBlocks.content:
That last row is why "just run the report against production" is wrong for a reason most people don't anticipate. It isn't only that the report is slow. **The report's scan evicts the transactional working set from the buffer pool.** Every till query that was being served from memory now goes to disk.

The report harms the tills far more than the tills harm the report. Add the MVCC bloat mechanism you worked through earlier, and one analyst can degrade a national checkout system.

**Options, in increasing cost and capability:** a dedicated analytics replica (cheap, isolates the buffer pool and the bloat problem, still row-oriented); a columnar warehouse fed by CDC or outbox (purpose-built, costs a pipeline and a freshness delay); materialised read models (fastest reads, least flexible).

**And then the part that is an architecture skill rather than a database skill.** Every one of these introduces staleness, so you must state the freshness the business is accepting — in writing, with a number:

- "Daily sales dashboard: data as of the last completed hour. Refreshed hourly."
- "Stock-on-hand for reordering: up to 15 minutes stale."
- "Fraud detection: under 30 seconds, because staleness here has direct monetary cost."

Writing these numbers down converts an invisible technical property into a business decision someone has agreed to. Without them, staleness is discovered by a finance director on a Tuesday.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Dual-writing to a second store.** No atomicity, silent divergence, no detection. Use an outbox or CDC.

**2. Building an outbox and forgetting the consumer must be idempotent.** At-least-once delivery is not a detail you can defer — the publisher *will* crash between publishing and marking sent.

**3. Treating a read model as a caching trick.** A cache can be discarded and repopulated on demand.
