2. **Which constraint is decisive?** Justify — and note that two of them pull in opposite directions.
3. Someone proposes JWTs with a 24-hour lifetime "so students don't keep logging in." State precisely what this costs in terms of the termination requirement, and quantify the exposure window.
4. Design the compromise. State the revocation window your design accepts, **who in the university has to formally accept it**, and what you would write in the ADR.
5. The wifi system's network isolation is not negotiable. How does this change your answer, and what does it tell you about deriving credential design from **topology** rather than preference?
6. A colleague suggests that since the IT team is only nine people, they should pick whichever option is simpler to operate. Assess that argument — it is not obviously wrong.
successCriteria: Comparison table populated with university specifics rather than restated generically — six systems, nine engineers, a stated legal window.
Identifies the tension explicitly: the six-system SSO requirement argues for tokens, the termination duty argues for sessions, and both are binding.
Quantifies the 24-hour proposal as up to a 24-hour exposure window after termination, and states that this fails a legal obligation measured in minutes.
Proposes short-lived access tokens (roughly 5–15 minutes) with a server-checked refresh token, and states the accepted revocation window as a specific number.
Names a role or function that must accept the window — HR, the data protection officer, or legal — rather than leaving it as an engineering decision.
Recognises that the wifi system's isolation makes a shared session store impossible for at least one consumer, so the topology decides the mechanism regardless of preference.

Engages seriously with the nine-person-team argument: operational simplicity is a legitimate constraint, but concludes that it cannot override a legal obligation, and ideally notes that a managed identity provider is how small teams get token infrastructure without operating it.

learningExperiences.title: Where Authorization Actually Happens

contentBlocks.content:
## What you'll be able to do after this

**Place authorization checks at the resource boundary**, and demonstrate why client-side or gateway-only enforcement is structurally insufficient.

Maps to `security-authn-authz` (mastery threshold **0.85** — this is one of the four raised-bar competencies) and `api-contract-design`.

## Authentication is *who are you*. Authorization is *may you do this*.

They are different, they fail differently, and only one of them is commonly enforced in the wrong place.

**As a front end engineer, this is the misconception most worth burning out of your instincts**, because your entire professional training has been about making the interface reflect what the user can do.

That reflection is a **courtesy**. The button is a suggestion. Anyone can open a terminal and issue the request the button would have issued.

> **Every authorization decision must be enforced at the resource, on the server, on every request.**

## Four layers, three of them insufficient

The newspaper's CMS. A contributor may edit **their own unpublished drafts**. An editor may edit anything.

**Layer 1 — the UI hides the edit button for others' drafts.** Necessary for usability. **Zero security value.** `POST /articles/9912` works fine from `curl`.

**Layer 2 — the API gateway checks the caller is authenticated.** Necessary. Establishes *who*. Says nothing about *whether they may edit this particular article*.

**Layer 3 — the handler checks `if (user.role === 'contributor' || user.role === 'editor')`.** Better, and still broken. It authorizes the **action type**, not the **specific resource**. Contributor A can edit contributor B's draft, because both are contributors.

This is **IDOR** — insecure direct object reference — and it is the single most common authorization bug in production systems.

contentBlocks.caption: Layer 4 — the correct check

contentBlocks.content:
Three things to notice.

**The check needs the resource itself**, so it can only happen *after* the fetch. This is why gateway-only enforcement is structurally insufficient: the gateway doesn't know who owns article 9912, and giving it that knowledge means duplicating your domain rules into the gateway, where they will drift.

**It encodes the actual rule, including the draft condition.** Rules that mention the resource's *state* cannot be expressed as role checks at all.

**It returns 404, not 403.** A 403 confirms the article exists, which leaks information: an attacker can enumerate valid IDs and learn what is in your unpublished pipeline. Return 404 for "exists but you may not see it" wherever existence itself is sensitive.

## Trust is a property of a boundary

The gateway validated the token at layer 2. But if an internal service is reachable by anything other than the gateway — a misconfigured network rule, a compromised sibling service, a developer's port-forward, a future service you haven't written yet — then **it is accepting unvalidated input.**

Trust is defined by **what can reach a component**, not by where you drew the arrows on the diagram.

terms.definition: Insecure direct object reference: authorizing the action type but not the specific resource, so any user of a role can access any instance of a resource.
A line across which callers or data must be re-validated, defined by what can actually reach a component rather than by the architecture diagram.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Authorizing by role instead of by resource.** `if (user.role === 'contributor')` lets every contributor edit every contributor's work. Check ownership *and* state, after fetching the resource.

**2. Returning 403 where 404 is appropriate.** A 403 confirms existence. Where existence is sensitive, return 404 for both "doesn't exist" and "not yours."

**3. Assuming the gateway's validation protects internal services.** Trust is defined by what can reach a component. Validate at every boundary.

**4. Forgetting inbound webhooks.** Your payment provider's webhook endpoint is on the public internet and anyone can POST to it. Without signature verification, anyone can mark any order paid. It *feels* internal because you built the integration — it is fully public.

**5. Caching an authorization decision without an invalidation path.** A revoked editor keeps editing until the TTL expires. Permission changes need explicit invalidation, because **the asymmetry runs toward granting access.**

**6. Writing the rule in the handler and also in the UI and also in a report generator.** Three copies drift. Put the rule in one place both call.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
**You get customer B's booking.** The check confirms you are *a* customer; it never asks whether you are *this booking's* customer.

What you need to try it: a terminal and a cookie. That's it. No tooling, no exploit, no special knowledge — just curl and an incremented integer. If the IDs are sequential you can enumerate the entire table, and if they're UUIDs you can still read any booking whose ID you have ever seen, which includes every one you've been shown in a shared link or an email.

This is IDOR, and it is consistently near the top of every real-world vulnerability ranking — not because it is subtle, but because the role check *looks* like authorization and passes review. You will exploit exactly this against your own code in this section's lab.
hints: What does the check actually verify, and what does it fail to verify?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A handler runs `if (user.role !== 'customer') return 403;` before returning a booking by ID. What is the flaw?
options: It should return 401 rather than 403 for an unauthorised request.
Nothing is wrong — the role check confirms the caller is a legitimate customer.
It authorizes the role but not the resource, so any customer can read any other customer's booking by changing the ID.
The check belongs in the API gateway so it is applied consistently across all endpoints.

optionFeedback.feedback: 401 means not authenticated; the user here is authenticated. It also addresses the status code while missing a much larger problem.
It confirms they are *a* customer, not that they are *this booking's* customer. That gap is the entire vulnerability.

Correct. This is an insecure direct object reference, the most common authorization bug in production systems. The check requires the resource itself, so it must happen after the fetch, and should return 404 where existence is sensitive.

The gateway does not know who owns a given booking, and giving it that knowledge duplicates domain rules where they will drift. Gateways enforce authentication and coarse policy; resource authorization lives with the resource.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Option D is worth dwelling on because it is a *sophisticated* wrong answer — centralising policy is genuinely good practice for coarse rules, and the instinct is sound. It fails here for a structural reason: **the gateway cannot evaluate a rule that depends on the resource, because it does not have the resource.** Any attempt to give it that knowledge duplicates your domain model outside your domain.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Your team caches a user's permission set for 10 minutes to avoid a database lookup per request. What is the failure, and why is the risk asymmetric?
options: No real failure — 10 minutes is a short window and permissions rarely change.

A revoked permission keeps granting access for up to 10 minutes; the risk is asymmetric because granting access you shouldn't is a security failure while withholding one briefly is an inconvenience, so revocation needs explicit invalidation with the TTL only as a backstop.
The risk is symmetric, so a shorter TTL of one minute resolves it adequately.
The correct control is to move the permission check to the API gateway so no cache is needed.

optionFeedback.feedback: Permissions change rarely and matter enormously when they do — specifically at the moment of an offboarding or a compromise, which is exactly when the window is being exercised.
Correct. Because the failure direction that matters is granting access, revocation must be **pushed** by the write path rather than waited out by a timer.
A shorter TTL shrinks the window without addressing that revocation should take effect immediately when it is issued.
A gateway cannot evaluate resource-level authorization, and this answer removes the cache without addressing revocation at all.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is the tiering-table asymmetry principle from earlier in this section, applied where the stakes are highest. **When the two failure directions have different costs, design asymmetrically**: let the cheap direction expire on a timer, and make the expensive direction push. Here the expensive direction is revocation, so revocation gets an explicit invalidation event.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt:
In your own words: **explain to a front end engineer why hiding the button is not security** — without being condescending about it, because hiding the button is genuinely the right thing to do for usability.

Then name the one grep you would run across a codebase to find likely IDOR bugs.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The framing that lands best is that the UI and the server are answering **different questions**. The UI answers "what should I offer this person?" — a usability question, and hiding the button is the correct answer to it. The server answers "may this request proceed?" — a security question, and it must answer independently, because the request can arrive without the UI ever being involved. Neither is a substitute for the other, and neither is wrong.

The grep: **look for role comparisons that are not followed by an ownership comparison.** Search for `user.role ===`, `hasRole(`, `roles.includes(`, or your equivalent, and for each hit ask whether the next few lines compare something on the *resource* to something on the *user*. Hits where they don't are your candidates.

It takes about ten minutes on a medium codebase and it finds real bugs in real systems — including, frequently, in code that has passed security review, because the role check reads as authorization to a reviewer skimming for its absence.
hints: What question is the UI answering, and what question is the server answering?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you?

workedExamples.problem: The newspaper's CMS must enforce: a contributor may edit **their own unpublished drafts**; an editor may edit anything. Work from the naive implementation to a correct one, and decide the status code.
steps: **Step 1 — start where teams start.** The UI hides the edit button on articles the user doesn't own. Necessary for usability, **zero security value** — `POST /articles/9912` works fine from a terminal.

**Step 2 — add gateway authentication.** The gateway verifies the caller's token and rejects anonymous requests. Necessary, and it establishes *who*. It says nothing about *whether they may edit this particular article*.

**Step 3 — add the role check, and notice it is still broken.** `if (user.role === 'contributor' || user.role === 'editor')` authorizes the **action type**, not the **resource**. Contributor A can edit contributor B's draft because both are contributors. This is IDOR.

**Step 4 — fetch the resource, then decide.** The rule mentions the article's owner *and* its state, so the check cannot run until the article is in hand: `isEditor || (isOwner && isDraft)`. Note that this is why the gateway structurally cannot do it — the gateway has no article.

**Step 5 — choose the status code deliberately.** Return **404**, not 403. A 403 confirms the article exists, letting an attacker enumerate IDs and learn what is in the unpublished pipeline. For a newspaper, an unpublished investigation is exactly the thing whose *existence* is sensitive.

**Step 6 — put the rule in one place.** The same rule will be needed by the UI (to decide whether to show the button), the API, and probably a reporting tool. Three copies drift, and the drift is silent. Express it once as a function both the UI-facing and API-facing paths call.

**Step 7 — verify by attacking it.** Log in as contributor A, take A's cookie, and request B's draft with curl. If you get data, the fix isn't done. This is not optional: a security control you have not attempted to bypass is a security control you have not tested.
workedExamples.conclusion: **Every authorization decision must be enforced at the resource, on the server, on every request** — and the check needs the resource itself, which is why it lives after the fetch and why no gateway can do it for you. Step 5 is the one most teams get wrong in the safe direction and never notice: returning 403 is more *informative*, and informativeness is precisely the problem when existence is sensitive. Step 7 is the one that turns a belief into a fact.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Why can an API gateway not fully enforce authorization? Give a specific rule that the gateway structurally cannot check, and explain what goes wrong if you try to give it the knowledge.
Why return 404 rather than 403 for a resource that exists but the caller may not see? Give one domain where the distinction matters a great deal.

learningExperiences.title: What the User Sees Inside the Window

contentBlocks.content:
## What you'll be able to do after this

**Describe the user-visible consequence of an eventual-consistency window and design a UX-safe mitigation.**

Maps to `state-caching-consistency` and `architecture-decision-communication`.

## Eventual consistency does not mean "sometimes wrong"

It means copies **converge after a delay**. The data isn't incorrect; it's from a moment ago.

The engineering task is to **bound the window and design what the user sees inside it.** That second half is a design activity, and it is usually skipped.

rows: user posts again — now there are two
**optimistic UI**: render the comment locally from the response; the user's own write is always shown to them
user believes payment failed, contacts support or pays twice
**route the entitlement read to the source of truth** for N seconds after purchase
**explicit purge on correction**, plus a short TTL as a backstop
user thinks the system is broken
contentBlocks.caption: Four windows, four mitigations — and all four mitigations are UX design rather than infrastructure.

contentBlocks.content:
## The principle worth memorising

> **A user must always see the effects of their own actions immediately. Other people's actions may be delayed.**

Almost every eventual-consistency complaint is a violation of the first half. Nobody is upset that someone else's comment took two seconds to appear; **everybody** is upset when their own does.

That asymmetry is why read-your-own-writes (`s7-database-systems`) is the guarantee that matters most in practice, despite being much weaker than linearizability.

## The cheapest fix in this entire course

That last table row deserves emphasis. Adding **"as of 14:05"** to a dashboard costs one line of code and eliminates an entire category of support tickets, because it converts an *invisible* property into a *stated* one.

This is `architecture-decision-communication` operating at the UI layer — and as a front end engineer, you are unusually well placed to notice where it's needed.

terms.definition: The property that copies converge after a bounded delay. Data from a moment ago, not incorrect data.
The guarantee that after you write something, you see it on your next read. The guarantee most often broken by naive replica routing.
The guarantee that a reader never sees time go backwards. What a price ticker needs even though it tolerates staleness.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Treating a staleness window as something users must tolerate.** The window is infrastructure; what the user sees inside it is design. Those are separable.

**2. Adding a loading spinner instead of showing the user's own write.** A spinner says "wait." Optimistic UI says "done." The user's own write is already known to have succeeded — you have the response.

**3. Optimistic UI without a failure path.** If the write later fails, the optimistic render must be reverted visibly, or you have shown the user something untrue and left it there.

**4. Applying read-your-own-writes to other people's writes too.** That is just routing everything to the primary, which discards the benefit.

**5. Hiding freshness because it looks unpolished.** "As of 14:05" reads as precision, not as an apology. Concealing it converts an understood property into a bug report.

**6. Never stating the window at all.** If nobody outside engineering knows the number, it will be discovered during a month-end close rather than agreed in a design review.

interactionSequence.prompt: A user adds an item to their cart and the cart badge still shows the old count for two seconds. A colleague says "that's just eventual consistency, users have to accept it." What is the strongest response?
options: They're right — bounded staleness is an unavoidable property of a distributed cache.
The window is infrastructure but what the user sees inside it is a design choice: the user's own write is already known to have succeeded, so render it immediately from the response.
Reduce the cache TTL to under one second so the window is imperceptible.
Route all cart reads to the primary database to eliminate staleness entirely.

optionFeedback.feedback: The window is unavoidable; showing the user a stale view of their own action is not. Conflating the two is what makes teams accept avoidable bad experiences.
Correct. This is the own-actions-versus-others principle: optimistic UI renders the badge locally from the successful response without waiting for the cached count to refresh.
This multiplies load on the source of truth to shrink a window that a design change eliminates entirely — and it still shows a stale value some of the time.
It works and it discards the cache's entire benefit for every read, including the vast majority that never needed the guarantee.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Options C and D are both *technically effective* and both solve a design problem by spending infrastructure. That pattern — reaching for a systems fix when a UI fix is available and better — is worth noticing in yourself. As a front end engineer you are unusually well placed to spot it.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt:
A subscriber pays for the newspaper. Their entitlement takes up to 5 seconds to propagate to the entitlement cache. During that window they refresh the article and **still see the paywall.**

**Trace what the user does next**, step by step, and estimate the cost to the business. Then propose the mitigation and say which of the four in the table it is.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The realistic sequence: refresh, still paywalled → conclude the payment failed → either **pay again** (now you have a duplicate charge, a refund process, and a support conversation) or **contact support** (a ticket, an agent, and a customer who now distrusts the checkout) or **abandon and request a refund** (you have lost the sale and the goodwill).

The cost is not the five seconds. It is a duplicate charge, a support ticket, and a subscriber whose first experience of paying you was that it appeared not to work.

The mitigation is row two: **route the entitlement read to the source of truth for N seconds after purchase** — read-your-own-writes, exactly the technique from `s7-database-systems`, applied at the caching tier rather than the replica tier. It costs a small amount of extra load on the source for a few seconds per purchase, which is trivially affordable given what it prevents.

Note that optimistic UI would *not* be the right answer here: you should not render the article as unlocked before the entitlement is confirmed, because unlike a comment count, being wrong in that direction gives away paid content.
hints: What does a user conclude when they pay for something and it does not appear?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

workedExamples.problem: The newspaper's comment system: a submitted comment takes up to 2 seconds to appear in the cached comment list. Users are double-posting. Design the fix, and decide what to do about the cases where optimistic UI is *not* appropriate.
steps: **Step 1 — identify whose action it is.** The user posted the comment. This is their own write, so the own-actions principle applies directly: they must see it immediately.

**Step 2 — recognise you already have the data.** The POST returned successfully and the response contains the created comment. You do not need to re-read anything to show it — the round trip to the cache is the *only* reason the user is waiting.

**Step 3 — render optimistically from the response.** Insert the comment into the local list immediately. The cached list catches up within 2 seconds and the subsequent refresh is invisible to the user.

**Step 4 — design the failure path, which is the step people skip.** If the write later turns out to have failed — a moderation rejection, a network error on a retry — the optimistic render must be **visibly reverted** with an explanation. Showing something untrue and leaving it there is worse than the original delay.

**Step 5 — decide the boundary case.** Other users' comments posted in the same window still take up to 2 seconds. That is fine and needs no mitigation: nobody is upset that a stranger's comment appeared two seconds late.

**Step 6 — identify where optimistic UI would be wrong.** Consider the paywall: rendering the article as unlocked before entitlement is confirmed would give away paid content on a failed payment. Where being wrong in the optimistic direction has a real cost, use **read-your-own-writes routing** instead — go to the source of truth for a few seconds rather than guessing.
**Step 7 — for anything that is neither, state the freshness.** A moderation queue or an analytics panel can simply say "as of 14:05." One line of code, and the staleness stops being a bug report.
workedExamples.conclusion: **A user must always see the effects of their own actions immediately; other people's actions may be delayed.** Step 6 is the important qualification: optimistic UI is the right tool when being wrong is cheap and recoverable, and the wrong tool when being wrong gives something away. The decision procedure is to ask **what it costs to be optimistically wrong** — cheap and reversible means render it, expensive or irreversible means route to the source, and neither means state the freshness.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Complete and explain: 'a user must always see the effects of ___ immediately; ___ may be delayed.' Then name the three mitigations and the question that selects between them.

learningExperiences.title: Practical: Cache It, Break It, Lock It Down

contentBlocks.content:
## What you'll be able to do after this

Reproduce a cross-user data leak, a stampede, and an IDOR vulnerability **in your own code**, then fix all three and verify the fixes.

The fifth commit on **Meridian**. Part C is the one that matters most: you will attack your own endpoint and get someone else's data.

## Part A — Tier the state (2 min)

Build the tiering table for Meridian's venue detail page. Include at minimum: venue description and photos, current availability for the next 30 days, the logged-in customer's name, this customer's saved payment methods, the venue's average rating, and the count of people currently viewing.

For each: **tier, TTL, key structure, invalidation trigger, and the staleness you are accepting** in words a product manager would understand. The last column is the deliverable that matters.

## Part B — Build and break the cache (4 min)

1. Cache the venue availability endpoint in a shared cache. Measure p99 and source query count under load.
2. **Break it #1 — the key.** Deliberately omit the date-range parameter from the key. Load-test with two different date ranges concurrently. Record how many responses contain the **wrong range's data.** Fix it.
3. **Break it #2 — the stampede.** Set a 30-second TTL, drive 2,000 rps, and record source query count per second **across the expiry boundary.** You should see hundreds or thousands of queries in one second.
4. Implement single-flight locking. Re-measure. Then implement stale-while-revalidate and measure again.
5. **Write down:** the query-count spike before and after each fix, and one sentence on which you would ship and why.

## Part C — Sessions and authorization (4 min)

1. Implement session-based auth with sessions in the shared cache. Cookie must be `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite=Lax`. **Regenerate the session ID on login.**
2. Implement the booking authorization rule: a customer may view and cancel **their own** bookings; a venue manager may view all bookings at **their** venues.
3. **Attack your own endpoint.** Log in as customer A. Using curl with A's cookie, request customer B's booking by ID. **If you get data, you have built the IDOR bug** — fix it and try again.
4. Verify the response for another customer's booking is a **404, not a 403.** Explain in one sentence what a 403 would leak.
5. Implement revocation: an admin action that terminates a user's session immediately. Verify with a request that was working one second earlier.

## Part D — Consistency window (2 min)

1. Introduce a deliberate 3-second delay between a booking being created and it appearing in the cached "my bookings" list.
2. Create a booking, then immediately view the list. Observe the experience.
3. Implement read-your-own-writes. Then implement optimistic UI as an alternative.
4. **Write down:** which is appropriate for which situation, and what each one does *not* fix.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors in this lab
contentBlocks.content:
**1. Skipping Part C step 3 because you 'know' the code is correct.** The whole point is that role checks look correct. Run the curl. Getting your own data back proves nothing — request *another user's* ID.

**2. Testing the stampede with a warm cache.** Flush the key immediately before the load test, or you will measure the hit path and see nothing.

**3. Load-testing Part B step 2 with one date range.** The leak only appears when two different inputs collide on one key.

**4. Forgetting `SameSite` and `Secure` on the cookie.** They are one line each and they are the difference between a session cookie and a liability.

**5. Implementing revocation but never testing it mid-session.** Revoke while a request is in flight and while a page is open. That is when it matters.

**6. Treating Part A as paperwork.** The staleness column is the deliverable — it is what you would actually take to a product manager, and it is what `s6-production-readiness-review` asks you to turn into an SLO.

interactionSequence.prompt:
Before Part B step 2: you will omit the date-range parameter from the cache key and load-test with **two different date ranges concurrently**.

**Predict what fraction of responses contain the wrong range's data.** Give a number.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
The answer is usually **close to half, and stable** — whichever range populated the key first is served to everyone until it expires, then the next miss re-populates it with whichever range happens to arrive first.

The stability is the dangerous part. It is not intermittent flickering that someone would notice and report as a glitch. It is a consistent wrong answer for the whole TTL, which means a developer checking the endpoint sees coherent behaviour and moves on.

Now substitute *user* for *date range* and you have the production version of this bug: one user's data served consistently to another for the length of the TTL. Same mechanism, and the only difference is which input you forgot.
hints: Which of the two ranges wins, and for how long?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that number?

interactionSequence.prompt: In Part C you attack your own endpoint with curl and successfully retrieve another customer's booking. What does this demonstrate about the value of the UI-level protection you also have?
options: The UI protection is broken and should be removed once the server check is added.
The UI protection was never a security control — it answers a usability question — and the server check is what answers the security question. Both should exist.
The UI protection is sufficient for most users, and the server check is defence in depth for sophisticated attackers.
The attack succeeded only because you had a valid session; without authentication the UI protection would have held.

optionFeedback.feedback: The UI protection is doing a useful job — deciding what to offer the user — and should stay. It simply was never the thing preventing unauthorised access.
Correct. Two components, two different questions: 'what should I offer this person?' and 'may this request proceed?' Neither substitutes for the other, and neither is wrong.
This frames it as a spectrum of attacker sophistication. It is not — changing an integer in a URL requires no sophistication at all, and the UI protection stops nobody who does it.
Authentication established who you are; it never established what you may access. That gap is the entire vulnerability, and it exists for every authenticated user.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Keep the curl transcript from before and after your fix. It is the single most persuasive artefact you will produce in this section — a two-line demonstration that a role check is not an authorization check — and it works on a skeptical reviewer far better than any explanation.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that answer?

interactionSequence.prompt:
You have now written an IDOR bug, exploited it, and fixed it — in about four minutes.

**Reflect: how many endpoints in a system you work on would survive the same curl?** You don't have to run it. Just count the endpoints that take a resource ID from the URL and ask yourself, for each, whether the handler compares that resource's owner to the caller.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
For most codebases the honest count is "more than zero, and I am not certain how many." That uncertainty is the useful output — it is much more actionable than a confident wrong answer in either direction.

The grep from earlier makes it tractable: find every role comparison and check whether an ownership comparison follows within a few lines. Ten minutes on a medium codebase, and it produces a list rather than a feeling.

Two things worth knowing before you raise it. First, this is not a criticism of whoever wrote the code — role checks read as authorization to a reviewer skimming for their absence, which is precisely why the bug is so common. Second, bring the curl transcript. A demonstration lands where a description does not, and you will be asked to demonstrate it anyway.

You will formalise this as an authorization sweep in `s6-production-readiness-review`, where it becomes part of a structured threat-boundary review rather than an ad-hoc grep.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you?

learningExperiences.title: Self-Guided: Read the Caching and Identity Decisions in Something You Use

contentBlocks.content:
## Why this one

Caching and identity decisions are unusually **visible from outside**. Response headers announce the TTL. Cookie flags announce the threat model. Timing a change announces the staleness window.

You are going to read one site's decisions from your own browser, and then do the harder thing: argue that each decision was reasonable given constraints you cannot see.

contentBlocks.title: Rules — read before starting
contentBlocks.content:
Stay entirely in **read-only observation of your own account and your own traffic.**

- Do not attempt to access anyone else's data.
- Do not test other people's accounts.
- Do not probe for vulnerabilities, enumerate IDs, or modify requests to see what happens.

Observing the headers your own browser receives is fine. Anything beyond that is not, regardless of intent — and "I was curious" is not a defence that has ever worked. The IDOR exercise in this section was on **your own code**, deliberately.

interactionSequence.prompt: After timing their revocation window in step 5: **which side of the sessions-versus-tokens trade did they choose, and what does the number tell you about what they optimised for?**

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
A logout on one device that terminates the other **within a second or two** indicates a server-side session or a checked revocation list — they chose revocability. A window of **several minutes** indicates short-lived tokens with a refresh mechanism, and the window is roughly the access-token lifetime. A window of **hours**, or one that never closes until the token expires, indicates long-lived tokens and a team that either accepted or did not consider that exposure.

What is genuinely informative is the *pairing*: a bank with a multi-minute window has made a different judgement from a social app with the same window, because the cost of a stolen session differs by orders of magnitude between them.

And note what you have just done — you measured a security property of a system you have no access to, using nothing but two devices and a stopwatch. That is a legitimate and surprisingly rare skill, and it is the same outside-in reasoning you practised on latency in Section 1.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you?

selfGuidedExercise.objective: Read a real product's caching tiers, staleness windows, and credential decisions from the outside, using only your own browser and your own account — then argue both sides of at least one decision you find.
selfGuidedExercise.realWorldContext: A site you use often and have an account with: a retailer, a social platform, a bank, a news site. You need an account because steps 3 and 5 involve observing your own writes and your own logout.
instructions: **Map the cache tiers.** In the Network tab, examine `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `Age`, and `Vary` headers on a dozen responses. Which resources are cached at the CDN — look for `Age` and CDN-specific headers? Which are `no-store`? Build a small table of resource → TTL → tier.

**Find the `Vary` header** on a personalised response. `Vary` is the cache key telling you which request headers change the output. What does its presence or absence tell you about what they consider safe to share?

**Find a staleness window.** Change something in your own account — update a profile field, add to a cart, post something — and time how long until it appears everywhere in the interface. Note any place it appears instantly in one view and lags in another. **That is a read-your-own-writes boundary, and you have just found where they drew it.**

**Examine the auth mechanism.** Session cookie or token? Check the cookie flags: `HttpOnly`? `Secure`? `SameSite`? If you can see a token in `localStorage`, note that — and note that you can see it, which is the point.

**Test revocation on your own account.** Log in on two devices. Log out or change the password on one. Time how long the other keeps working. That number is their revocation window, measured empirically.
Write 300–500 words presenting your findings as if briefing a colleague.

**Then the important part.** For at least one decision, argue *both* that it was correct given their likely constraints **and** what you would want to know before agreeing. Practising both sides of the same decision is the habit `architecture-decision-communication` is built on.
materialsOrPrerequisites: A browser with developer tools, and an account you own on the site you choose.
A second device or a second browser profile, for the revocation test.
A stopwatch or a clock — the staleness and revocation measurements are timings.
reflectionPrompts: Where did they draw the read-your-own-writes boundary, and can you find a view where they drew it in the wrong place?
What do their cookie flags tell you about the threat model they are designing against?
Did you find a `Vary` header that surprised you — either present where you did not expect personalisation, or absent where you did?
For the decision you argued both sides of: which side did you find harder to argue, and what does that tell you about your own defaults?

verification.mode: self-assessment against criteria, with the write-up retained for the design review in the final section
selfAssessmentCriteria: I stayed within read-only observation of my own account and my own traffic throughout.
I built a resource-to-tier table from actual response headers rather than from assumption.
I measured a staleness window by timing my own change, and identified where their read-your-own-writes boundary sits.
I recorded their cookie flags and can say what threat each one addresses.
I measured their revocation window empirically and inferred which side of the credential trade they chose.
I argued both sides of at least one decision, and the weaker side is a real argument rather than a token one.

sections.title: Splitting the System and Surviving It
sections.description: Splitting a system relocates complexity from inside one process to the network between processes. This section decides whether that trade is worth making — evaluating topologies against team structure rather than fashion, drawing boundaries by business capability, choosing sync or async per interaction with the availability arithmetic attached, and then engineering for the partial failures that distribution creates: timeouts, jittered retries, idempotency keys, circuit breakers, bulkheads, failure domains, and graceful degradation. Teaching examples come from a restaurant group; the transfer exercises move to a container port terminal.

learningObjectives.description: Evaluate monolith, modular monolith, and multi-service topologies against team size, change cadence, and coupling, naming the trigger and the largest cost accepted.
Draw service boundaries by business capability and defend them against a layer-based split, using the change-cadence, data-ownership, and transactional tests.
Choose synchronous request/response or asynchronous messaging per interaction, stating the delivery and ordering guarantees required and the availability cost of each synchronous link.
Apply timeouts, bounded retries with jittered backoff, and idempotency keys to make a cross-service write safe to repeat under an ambiguous timeout.
Identify a system's failure domains and design a graceful-degradation path that preserves core function, distinguishing engineering decisions from business ones.
Estimate load and storage from product numbers and name the binding bottleneck before proposing any scaling strategy.

motivationHooks.prompt:
## Why this matters

There is a specific career moment this section prepares you for. You'll be in a room where someone says *"we should break this into microservices,"* and everyone will nod, because it sounds like what grown-up companies do.

If you can't articulate what you'd be buying and what you'd be paying, you will either agree to a two-year project that makes everything worse, or object on instinct and lose the argument.

The honest position: **splitting a system does not reduce complexity. It relocates complexity from inside one process — where it is visible, debuggable, and transactional — to the network between processes, where it is none of those things.** Sometimes that trade is excellent. Sometimes it is catastrophic.

And that failure handling is the other half of this section. The moment you make a network call, you inherit a new category of problem. A function call either returns or throws. A network call can return, throw, hang forever, succeed slowly, or — the one that ruins your week — **time out after having actually done the work.**

**Commit to an answer before you begin.**

Your checkout calls five services synchronously. Each one is individually reliable: 99.95%, 99.9%, 99.5%, 99.0%, and 99.7% available.

**What is checkout's availability ceiling, in minutes of downtime per month?**

Write down a number. Most engineers estimate something close to the worst individual dependency — around 99%, or seven hours. The real figure is **about 14 hours**, and the intervention that fixes it makes no single component more reliable.

You call a payment service. Three seconds pass. Your timeout fires.

**You do not know whether the customer was charged.**

There are three possible states of the world and they are indistinguishable from where you are standing. Every retry strategy that assumes one of them is wrong a third of the time — and one of those thirds is a duplicate charge.

## Back to the availability chain

Availabilities in a synchronous chain **multiply**:

0.9995 × 0.999 × 0.995 × 0.99 × 0.997 ≈ **0.9805**

That is **98.05%**, or roughly **14 hours of downtime per month** — from five dependencies that each look perfectly respectable in isolation.

If you estimated around 99%, you anchored on the worst dependency. The chain is worse than its weakest link, because every link fails independently.

Now the intervention. Three of those five calls — loyalty, recommendations, email — are things **no customer waits for.** Convert them to asynchronous messaging and they leave the availability chain entirely. Checkout's ceiling rises to about **99.85%**, or roughly 65 minutes a month.

**No dependency became more reliable.** You simply stopped requiring three of them to be up in order to take money. That is why converting a synchronous call to an asynchronous one is usually the cheapest availability improvement available to you — and why sync-versus-async is an availability decision rather than a stylistic one.

sectionSummary.content:
## What you should now believe

**Microservices solve organisational problems, not technical ones.** Independent deployment, independent scaling, team autonomy. A team of eight has none of those problems and will pay every cost. The modular monolith — enforced module boundaries, exclusive data ownership per module — is usually the right answer, and it makes a later split mechanical.

**Boundaries follow business capability, not technical layer.** Trace one feature and count the hops: a layer-based split crosses every service for every feature, which is a distributed monolith. Two services writing the same table is the clearest signal a boundary is wrong.

**Sync or async is decided per interaction, not per service pair**, by asking whether the caller needs the answer to proceed. Every synchronous call is a link in an availability chain, and availabilities multiply.

**"Async" is not "don't await."** Dropping the await gives you a lost request with no durability, no retry, and no visibility. Real messaging needs a durable intermediary and four explicit decisions.

**A timeout is more dangerous than an error.** Three possible states, indistinguishable from the caller. Only a client-generated idempotency key resolves it — and retries without one are worse than no retries at all.

**Degradation is preserved core function, not a nicer error message.** The row of your degradation table with no answer is your true single point of failure; the row that is a business judgement should be escalated before the outage, not during it.

**Estimate before you propose.** The arithmetic usually says the system is smaller than it feels, and the load that dominates is usually not the one the business talks about.
keyTakeaways: Try the cheap fix first: test coverage, feature flags, and faster CI are weeks; decomposition is quarters.
Three boundary tests: change cadence, exclusive data ownership, transactional need. The third usually decides.
Availabilities in a synchronous chain multiply — five 99.x% dependencies is roughly 98%.
The complete call pattern: timeout + bounded jittered retry + idempotency key + circuit breaker + bulkhead.
Retries and idempotency keys ship together or not at all — one without the other converts a loud failure into a silent, expensive one.
A bad deploy is a failure domain, and it is the one you control most directly.
Propose changes only against the binding bottleneck, and name its number before you propose anything.

furtherReading.title: MonolithFirst
furtherReading.citation: Fowler, Martin. "MonolithFirst." martinfowler.com, 2015.
furtherReading.author: Martin Fowler
furtherReading.rationaleNote: The canonical short argument for starting monolithic, including the observation that early boundaries are usually wrong. Read it alongside the companion piece on the microservice premium — together they make the case this section's topology experience argues, from someone who has watched many teams get it wrong in both directions.

furtherReading.title: Release It! — Stability Patterns
furtherReading.citation: Nygard, Michael T. "Release It! Design and Deploy Production-Ready Software," 2nd edition. Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2018.
furtherReading.author: Michael T. Nygard
furtherReading.rationaleNote: The origin of circuit breakers and bulkheads as named patterns, and the best available collection of real failure narratives. Read the stability antipatterns chapter if you want to understand *why* one dependency's failure spreads — the mechanisms are more varied than this section had room for.

furtherReading.citation: Brooker, Marc. "Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter." Amazon Builders' Library.
furtherReading.author: Marc Brooker
furtherReading.rationaleNote: A rigorous treatment of exactly the pattern in this section's retry worked example, including the mathematics of why jitter matters and how retry storms form. Short, practical, and written by people operating this at very large scale.
